Uniform Title: Tārārahasyavṛtti 2 Author: Brahmānanda Manuscript: NGMCP Manuscript No.: A-1337 Reel No.: D 28/26

Description: Description by Mark S.G. Dyczkowski: The *Śrīmat-Paramārthasāra* (The Essence of the Supreme Reality) is a concise treatise on non-dual Śaiva philosophy attributed to Abhinavagupta. It is composed in the form of a dialogue between a teacher and a disciple, consisting of fifty-seven verses. The work serves as a summary of the essential doctrines of Trika Śaivism, focusing on the nature of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), the process of cosmic manifestation (*sṛṣṭi*), the means of liberation (*upāya*), and the state of liberation itself (*mokṣa*). Through its elegant and systematic exposition, it elucidates the identity of the individual soul (*puruṣa*) with the supreme consciousness (*parā saṃvit*), emphasizing that all diversity arises from and returns to this singular, self-luminous source. The text concludes by defining the liberated state as the realization of one's own innate sovereignty (*svātantrya*) and the cessation of all dualistic thought.

The *Tārārahasya*, for which this is a commentary, was composed in Bengal by Brahmānanda in the Śaka year 1735, corresponding to 1659 CE. It concerns the worship of the goddess Tārā, who is regarded as a form of Kālī, though she was originally a Buddhist deity. This manuscript of the *Tārārahasyavṛtti* appears to be a distinct version of the *Tārārahasyavṛttikā* by Gauḍīya Śaṅkarācārya, which is already available among the e-texts at Muktabodha. While the identity of the two texts is discernible, the differences between them are so substantial that they merit separate consideration and comparison.

Oṃ. Homage to the venerable Guru Gaṇeśa.
Homage to the venerable Bhavānī.
I bow to Mahānīlasarasvatī, who is dense with intense bliss, who embodies the form of all the gods, and who possesses the nature of the Supreme Mother (Parāmbā).
Having understood the Nīlatantra, the supreme Siddhasārasvata,
the Vīratantra, the Matsyasūkta, the Gāruḍa, and likewise the Bhairavī;
Having understood the intention of his Guru, Śrī Śaṅkara indeed composed this commentary on the *Tārārahasya*, which is endowed with the essence of all the Āgamas.
For the sake of successfully accomplishing all rites, the worship and other practices are now written down;
in the first chapter, the daily worship of the Goddess was revealed.
In the second chapter, first, is the specific procedure for initiation;
in the third, however, is the preliminary practice (*puraścaryā*) by which the status of being a mantra-holder is attained.
The Naimittika [rite] occurs in the fourth [chapter], while the determination of the Kāmya [rites] is in the fifth;
the determination of the Rahasya is in the sixth, and likewise, the Kumārī [rite] is in the seventh.
In the eighth [chapter], the preliminary rites (puraścaryā) of Tārā are proclaimed;
in the ninth chapter, there is the definitive determination of the mantras of the Goddess.
In the tenth chapter is the hymn, and likewise the fruit in the eleventh;
in the twelfth chapter is the thorough determination of meditative cultivation (bhāvanā).
The ritual for daily worship is in the thirteenth chapter,
while the correct procedure for the fire offering (homa) of Tārā is in the fourteenth.
In the fifteenth [chapter], however, is the determination of the reality of the latent impressions of mantras;
thus concludes the *Tārārahasya*, the definitive exposition on meditation.

Then, having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, one should meditate upon Kuṇḍalinī— who consists of the Root-Mantra (*mūlavidyā*) and is as formidable as ten million suns— within the lotus of the *mūlādhāra*, and [lead her] through the *suṣumnā* into the supreme splendor of Brahman.
One should cause the consciousness, which has become restless through the stream of nectar at the junction of the *marmas*, to descend again to the *mūlādhāra*.
And thus says the Śruti:
"Shining forth at the first departure, becoming as if immortal upon every return."
I take refuge in her whose form is bliss, who moves along the inner path.
Having arisen from that, one should perform the necessary duties.
This is stated in the Matsyasūkta: [p.
Having risen during the final watch of the night and meditated upon Kuṇḍalinī as the form of the syllable *ḍiḍā*,
a man shall become a perfected being (*siddha*) and attain mastery over the vital breath (*svara*).
Also in the Nīlatantra:
Having risen during the final watch of the night, one should meditate on the fierce Tāriṇī,
as subtle as a thread, extending from the mūlādhāra to the brahmarandhra.
She is the embodiment of the root mantra itself, manifest as the form of nectar and bliss;
she outshines ten million suns and is as cool as ten million moons.
Resembling ten million flashes of lightning above the crest of the bliss of desire,
his body is enveloped by the mass of its radiance and rendered pale-red.
Endowed with all auspiciousness, one should perform the rite of bathing;
having taken earth and *kuśa* grass, one should then go to the water's edge.
Having bathed to remove impurities, one should perform the mantra-bath;
having immersed oneself thus three times with the Vidyā, one should sip water for the pacification of sin.
At the end of the root mantra, one should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) with the word "tarpayāmi" followed by "svāhā"; this is the prescribed method for the libation.
Performing it thus three times results in the destruction of all sins.

Then, when the time for bathing has arrived, having bathed according to the prescribed rule and performed the libation (tarpaṇa), one should perform the libation three times with the formula: "I offer libations to Śrī Nīlasarasvatī," or "I offer libations to Śrī Ugratārāmbā," or "I offer libations to Ekajaṭāmbā," ending each with the root mantra.
Having placed kuśa grass, the penis, flowers, sandalwood flowers, kuśa, and unbroken rice— each measuring one *prastha*— into a small vessel, one should offer the *argha*.
At the end of the root mantra: *udyadādityavartinyai śivacaitanyamayyai svāhā*. This is the mantra.
Having thus offered the water for the feet (*argha*) to the Sun as remembered, one should then perform the ritual worship (*pūjā*).
One should visualize the Goddess within the solar disc.

Then, an *arghya* offering is presented— consisting of *bilva* fruit, unbroken rice (*akṣata*), hibiscus flowers (*javā*), red sandalwood, and *vajra*-flowers— either with the *Gāyatrī* or with the root mantra (*mūlavidyā*).
As it is said in the Kālikātantra:
"O Bhagavatī, O Eka-jaṭā, we know thee; O Vi-kaṭa-daṃtā, we meditate upon thee; may that Tārā inspire us."
Then, having meditated upon [the deity] in the heart and recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, one should proceed to a body of water.
Thus it is said in the Phetkāriṇī Tantra:
"In a solitary liṅga, or in a cremation ground, or in an empty house, or at a crossroads..."
Abiding there, the yogi should accomplish the Vidyā Tribhuvaneśvarī.
In that regard:
where no other linga is seen within a distance of five krośas, that is declared to be an ekaliṅga; there, supreme accomplishment (siddhi) is attained.
Regarding the characteristics of a crossroads, another tantra states:
"One should recognize a crossroads where a stone of Tāriṇī resides;
there, those desiring accomplishment should diligently perform ritual service and recitation."
Elsewhere also: "In a thicket, or on a mountain, or in a deserted place,
at a crossroads, in a temple, or in an empty, secluded, and lovely dwelling."
Thus, regarding the locations:
in the *Vīratantra*,
it is said that if a person recites [the mantra] in an empty house, a cremation ground, at a single *liṅga*, by a pond, or in a temple on the banks of the Gaṅgā...
One who possesses a mind purified from impurities by the mountain-like [scriptures], who is always endowed with devotion,
who worships the Lord of the World— the source of knowledge, glory, and the blue [light]— and who understands the meaning of all the teachings, becomes a preeminent yogi at the end of the body.
One attains the state of supreme Śiva, which is Brahman, the Nirvāṇa.
Thus, having resorted to the respective locations, one should contemplate the sacred seat (pīṭha) therein.
This has been stated in the Gāndharva Tantra:
Having meditated upon a cremation ground there, one should visualize a wish-fulfilling tree (kalpadruma) at that spot;
at its root is a jeweled pedestal adorned with various gems.
Adorned with various ornaments and decorations, and graced by the gods of the root-mantras,
it is surrounded on all sides by auspicious female spirits who delight in flesh and bones.
In the four directions, [one should place] the limbs of corpses, adorned with funeral pyre ashes and bones;
in their center, one should meditate upon the Goddess according to the yoga of the prescribed visualization.
Having meditated thus:
*oṃ vajrodake hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*, having empowered that water; and with *oṃ hrīṃ svāhā*, having washed one's hands and feet; [one recites] *oṃ hrīṃ suviśuddhadharma sarvapāpāṇi*.
"May my mental constructs be removed! HŪM PHAṬ SVĀHĀ.
Having thus sipped water, [one performs] the binding of the topknot with: "OṂ MAṆIDHARI VAJRIṆI SARVAVAŚAṂKARI HŪM PHAṬ SVĀHĀ."

"Rakṣa 2 svāhā"— by this consecration with water, the purification of the ground is accomplished. Reciting "Oṃ sarvavighnānutsāraya hūṃ phaṭ svāhā," one should scatter unbroken grains (*akṣata*) and, using the *anuttara* and *nānā* mudrās, drive away the three types of obstacles.
Oṃ apavitra vajrabhūme hūṃ phaṭ svāhā—having thus consecrated the ground with water, [sprinkle] it with that water.

There, having spread out soft, extensive, and gentle cushions, one should invoke and worship that [seat] with red sandalwood and flowers while reciting "Ā ĀḤ SUREKHE VAJRAKHE HŪṂ PHAṬ SVĀHĀ," and then sit there according to the sequence of the svastika and other postures.
This has been stated in the Matsyāsūkta:
Seated upon a soft woolen blanket or on other comfortable seats,
and remaining well-seated, one should accomplish the supreme siddhi.
In battle, having drunk liquor such as *vyādika* and the like, one who dies within six months will attain [the state of] *sita* near the funeral pyre or in its vicinity.

The meaning of this is as follows: from ten months until six months have passed; "garbhacyuta-bālaka" means a child who has fallen from the womb; "acūḍaka" means one for whom the cūḍākaraṇa ceremony has not been performed.

From the time of the *upanayana* until before the *cūḍākaraṇa*, their ritual procedure is gentle and unelaborate; in the absence of these [materials], it is performed on a seat (*viṣṭara*) or upon *kuśa* grass.
As it is stated in the *Śrīkrama*:
O beloved, if the *vīrāsana* is unavailable, listen to the description of the *mṛtāsana*:
a deceased child who has not yet reached five years of age, one whose tonsure ceremony (*cūḍā*) has been performed within six months, or one who died before reaching ten months.

A child accompanied by the *garbha* [mantra], preceded by the eight *śṛgarbhas*—this is the *komalavidyā*. [It should be performed] on *havistara* grass or upon *kuśa* grass. As it is stated in the *Matsyasūkta*:
One should prepare a seat from the skin of a black antelope or a leopard, with the hair on the inner side intact, and it may be yellow, white, or blue.

Now, however, [the seat] may be a grass mat (*viṣṭara*) or else coiled (*kuṇḍalīkṛta*). Thus, having propitiated the secret of the seat, it should be understood from the mouth of the Guru. Reciting "Oṃ maṇidharaṇi vajriṇi mahāvajriṇi mahāpratisare rakṣa 2 māṃ huṃ phaṭ svāhā," one should tie a protective thread at the edge of the garment.
Oṃ āḥ hūṃ āḥ hūṃ svāhā. With these two hands, for the pervasive binding, this is the purification of speech and mind.
Oṃ namaḥ puṣpaketu-rājārhate tathāgatāya samyaksaṃbuddhāya. Puṣpe puṣpe.
"O Mahāpuṣpe, Supuṣpe, Bhūṣitapuṣpe, and Yāvakīrṇe, hūṃ phaṭ svāhā!
Having thus performed the mantra for the flowers and other offerings, [one should place them] upon a seat made of gold or other materials,
which has been smeared with red sandalwood, gorocanā, saffron, vajra-flowers, and so forth.
With the mantra *oṃ āḥ sulekhe vajrarekhe hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*, one should draw the night [mandala], which consists of four gates and contains an eight-petaled lotus within a downward-facing triangle.
And it is said in the Cūḍāmaṇi:
"Then, having diligently fashioned a pedestal with the *kula-rasa*..."
Aṃ āḥ surekhe hūṃ phaṭ, and likewise the pair [hūṃ phaṭ].
One should draw a beautiful eight-petaled lotus with this mantra.

On the eastern petal of that lotus, one should write *hrīṃ*; on the southern, *trīṃ*; on the northern, *pha*; on the western, *ṭa*; and in the center of the triangle, one should write *hūṃ*. This has been stated in the *Pheravītantra*:

He should then prepare a seat of soft materials and, having sat upon it, write the mantra with sandalwood paste on a lotus of eight petals; he should then write the *māyā* syllable on the eastern petal.
The central seed-syllable is in the second [position], while the speech is in the north and west;
one should write the central seed-syllable, O Nārada, and then perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi).

*Tāraṃ* refers to the *huṃkāra*, because it is well known that the *tāra* (the syllable *oṃ*) is the salutation for *Tārā*. Alternatively, in the ritual procedure (*vidhāna*) for the fierce *Nīlasarasvatī*, it refers to the *sādhya-tāra* (the *oṃ* of the one to be accomplished).
Alternatively, according to the ritual procedure for Ugrā Nīlasarasvatī, some maintain that there is a *tāra* (the syllable Om) in the center;
others say there is a lotus marked with a hexagon in the middle.
This has been stated in the Gāndharva [Purāṇa]:
Immediately after the hexagon, there is a lotus and again two earth-mandalas;
in their center, one should worship the invocation of the goddesses.
Thus, the writing of the seed-syllable (bīja) is as before, preceded by the earth-element. In that very context, there is this distinction:
one should write the seed-syllable of the *preta* at the end of the hexagon, together with the corpse, as previously described.
However, for those seeking the Sarasvata [attainment], a specific procedure has been stated in another tantra.
As it is said in the Nīlatantra:

The yantra of the one whose body is blossoming is encircled by a house; it measures two *vyāmas* [in length], is adorned with a pair of ears marked by the letters *rasa*, *nārṇa*, and *ka*, and is beautified by a mass of shimmering filaments (*kesara*) and a covering cloth upon the earth.
It shines with the water-like luster of the Lord of the Stars (the Moon) and is graced by two triangles.
It has been declared that this bestows the accomplishment of all aims.
Thus, having placed one of these [texts], such as the *Gambhīrā*, upon a pedestal (*pīṭha*) in front of the Viracarya, one should worship the pedestal with:
*oṃ hūṃ śmaśānāyai namaḥ*.
To the golden tree, twice. At its root: Oṃ, to Peace, twice; Oṃ, to Flowers, twice; Oṃ, to Ṣṭhau, twice;
Oṃ, to the Jewel-Throne, twice; Oṃ, homage to the various jewels; Oṃ, homage to the various ornaments, twice.
To the gods, twice. Oṃ, to the laughing jackals with many months-old bones, twice.
Oṃ, to the corpses, skulls, funeral pyres, embers, and bones, twice. In the four directions. Then, on the eight petals:
Oṃ, obeisance to Lakṣmī; Oṃ, to Sarasvatī, twice; Oṃ, to Rati, twice; Oṃ, to Kānti, twice; Oṃ, to Puṣṭi, twice; Oṃ, to Tuṣṭi, twice.

Having thus worshipped [the deity] in the northern direction, one should arrange the seat for the Great Preta with the mantra *hmau mahāpretāsanāya namaḥ* at its base. This has been stated in the *Siddhisārasvata*:
Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Ratī, Prīti,
Kīrti, Śānti, Puṣṭi, and Tuṣṭi— these are the eight Śaktis.
The misfortunes of the goddess Nīlasarasvatī are destroyed by the *pīṭhaśaya*.
Likewise, in the Vīratantra:
"In the midst of that, one should worship the invocation of the goddess and the *trāva* itself."
Thus ends the sequence for the worship of the *pīṭha*. Now, the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*). [Recite] *yathā...

stāya phaṭ*. Having thoroughly cleansed both hands, perform the snapping of fingers (*choṭikā*), the three claps (*tāla*), and the binding of the ten directions (*daśadigbandhana*) with that same [mantra].
Then, performing the regulation of breath (*prāṇāyāma*) and forming the hand-gestures (*mudrā*) with the limbs, [proceed] from the *ādhāra* with the mantra *ahaṃ saḥ*.
The Kuṇḍalinī leads the individual soul from the heart through the twenty-five principles by way of the Suṣumnā path; I shall unite it with the Supreme Radiance through the Kumbhaka breath-retention.

Having meditated on the syllable *jhaṃ* at the navel, one should contemplate one's own body being consumed by the fire arising from it; then, having contemplated the syllable *ka* as the seat (*pīṭha*) in the heart, one should disperse that ash with the wind arising from it;
finally, having contemplated the white-colored syllable *hūṃ* at the head, one should wash those bones with the water arising from it.
Having made the entire body free from impurity, one should immerse it in me. Then, one should contemplate oneself as having gone to that stainless state through the differentiation of the deity. (p.

In that all-pervading water, having meditated on a red lotus from the syllable *āḥ*, one should contemplate a white lotus from the syllable *dāṃ* above it; and above that, having visualized the syllable *hūṃ* resembling the color of a blue lotus, one should meditate on the pericarp adorned with the seed-syllable *hrīṃ*.
One should install and meditate [upon the deity] while reciting "Ā HŪṂ KRAU SVĀHĀ" eleven times.
This is stated in the *Phetkārīya*:
"Having visualized the Māyā-syllable at the navel as red in color, one should [burn away impurities] with the fire born from it."
Then, one should contemplate the body as dried up by sin and consumed by fire.
Having caused the ashes to be swept away by the wind arising from that yellow syllable *trāṃ* at the heart,
one should then contemplate [the syllable] on the forehead.
Having caused those [bones] to become white as snow through nectar,
one should contemplate oneself as being flooded by that [nectar).
It is completely free from all suffering, stainless, and of the nature of the deity;
it pervades the universe and proceeds toward the pericarp arising from the source of sound.
Having meditated upon a syllable *hūṃ* resembling the color of a dark blue cloud above that, one should meditate on *kartṛkas* (surgical knives) adorned with the seed-syllable *hūṃ*.
Above those, one should meditate on Kharvā, who is as blue as a fresh rain-cloud and has a protruding belly.

Her waist is covered with a tiger skin; she has thick, protruding breasts, three round red eyes, a lolling tongue, and a terrifying face with bared fangs; her single matted lock is tawny and fierce, hanging down on both sides above it.

He wears a garland of blue lotuses and has matted hair as dark as a black serpent; his forehead is adorned with a band of white bone and three skull-cups, and he has earrings made of the *takṣaka* serpent that resemble flowers.
She wears necklaces made of exceedingly white serpents and a crown made of dark-green lotus petals;

her matted locks are fixed upon a fist adorned with pieces of raw flesh mixed with blood, and her hand is decorated with a fierce sword whose hilt is attached to the top [of the hair]. Her [lotus] stalk is slightly red...

May the Mother, whose left hand holds a blooming blue lotus, whose lower right hand is adorned with the seed-syllable, and whose hand is decorated with a round knife, remove the dullness of my three worlds and adorn my hands with brilliance.
Her armlets are made of smoke-colored serpents, her bracelets of gold-colored serpents;

she is mounted upon a corpse with the intent of thoroughly restraining it, her right foot drawn back against the heart of the corpse while her left foot is extended, resting upon both feet of the corpse; her waist is adorned with a girdle made of jasmine-white serpents.

She wears slightly reddened nāga-skin anklets; her two lotus feet are adorned with a garland of fifty-four human heads, which are bound together by their hair and from which streams of fresh blood are still flowing.
Seated upon the center of a blazing fire-altar, her waist bound with a leopard skin, adorned with all the ornaments of a woman,
her head graced by Akṣobhya, and her face smiling with intense passion— thus [she is visualized].
"One should meditate on form as the self"—this is the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*).
As it is stated in the *Rudrayāmala*:
"One should contemplate its form, which is devoid of qualities, as if it were one's own heart."
Also in the *Nīlatantra*:
"Then, having performed the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), one should contemplate the entire universe as empty;
[one should contemplate] oneself as pure, free from taints and qualities, consisting of Tāriṇī."

Then, one should meditate upon a red lotus arising from the syllable Āḥ in the intermediate space; furthermore, one should meditate upon the syllable HŪṂ, resembling the color of a dark cloud, above that.
Then, from the seed-syllable *huṃ*, one should meditate upon oneself as Tāriṇī, adorned with the seed-syllable of the knife (*karttarī*) and seated upon a corpse.
The mode of meditation:
[one should visualize her] with feet in the *pratyālīḍha* stance, terrible, adorned with a garland of severed heads,
dwarfish, with a protruding belly, fearsome, and wearing a tiger skin around her waist.
Endowed with fresh youth and adorned with the five mudrās,
[the faces] are the beautiful face, the square, the round, and the ox-face.
The five mudrās are renowned as the *yonimudrā* when performed with salutations;
she has four arms, a protruding tongue, is most formidable, and bestows boons.
Her two right arms are joined with a sword and a chopper,
and her pair of left hands are endowed with a skull-cup and a blue lotus.
"In the chapter on the one with tawny hair and a topknot, she is adorned with Akṣobhya upon her crown";
"adorned with five" means she is endowed with a white bone band on the forehead and a garland of five skulls— thus it is stated in the *Śivadīkṣāṭikā*, which is included within the *Mantrasāra*.

By that [verse] beginning with "sumukham" and ending with "namaskṛtau," indeed, Śaṅkarācārya has also stated in the *Bhagavatī* that she alone possesses a skull with various bones and five [faces] on her forehead, while Akṣobhya is upon her crown.
Regarding the term "vibhūṣitām" (adorned):
the commentator states that Akṣobhya, who is imperishable, is the crescent moon upon the crown of the head (*maulau mastake*).
Therefore, O Mistress who has the moon as her crest-ornament, because [you] have not been mentioned in any meditation manual.
In reality, however,
having taken up the mantra of the Goddess, the Guru remains in the form of the serpent Vāsuki as the protector of the youth; thus he is also called "Jūṭa."
Thus, from hearing the words of the Matsya-sūkta; for this very reason, in this tradition, Akṣobhya is stated to be the seer (ṛṣi). In the Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi:
"Akṣobhya-nāga, Akṣobhya-devī, the three-formed one who assumes the form of a nāga upon the head."
Thus one should meditate for the sake of accomplishing all aims; the scripture conducive to such meditation is as follows:
Having gone to a deserted dwelling and sat down upon a corpse-seat or similar seat,
having driven away obstacles with a single-pointed mind, one should then contemplate the universe as being of the nature of consciousness.

Then, having performed the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) by means of the seed-syllables (*bīja*) and having gone there into the sky, one should meditate upon one’s own self as the enemy of Māra, consisting of the syllable *HŪṂ* in an exalted state. With that [syllable] acting as a sword, one should [sever] the meaning of contradictory statements;
and with the circle of fire, [one should see her] whose belly is bent by the qualities of the clouds of speech, exceedingly short, yet not lacking in youth.

Standing upon a corpse with her legs bound by a tiger positioned below, she rests atop many corpses of great majesty; wearing a garland of severed heads, she stands in the *ūrdhvamālīḍha* posture upon a lotus.
Her three eyes were reddened by the mass of entrails emerging from the formidable head-crests of her shattered, multi-colored skulls.
She is resplendent with a single matted lock of hair tawny from its undivided state, adorned with ornaments of bone and terrifying with a human skull;
she truly manifests the eight great supernatural powers as her own adornments, and with her loud, boisterous laughter, she strikes terror into the worlds.
Ananta is her matted locks, Takṣaka and Mahāpadma are her two earrings, and Padma is the ornament of her necklace upon her heart;
likewise, Karkoṭaka serves as her sacred thread, and O Lord, Vāsuki is her beautiful girdle.
O Śaṅkhapāla, Kaṅkaṇa is not considered [to reside] in the feet; Padma is in the ankles, and Nūpura is in the shanks.
Ujjeṣu is considered to be in the thighs, and Kulika is in the upper arms; the Anujas are considered to be in the bones of the necklaces.
Black, red, white, and likewise dark-blue, yellow, ash-colored, and pale—
these are the species of serpent-crests here, all of them blazing with jewels.
She always holds with her own manly arms a skull, a chopper, a knotted and fierce mass of hair, a garland possessing the luster of a blue lotus,
and hundreds of unsheathed swords.

One who beholds her lotus feet— she who shines with the two and five mudrās, who possesses a garland of blue lotuses, who bestows the power of poetry, who fulfills the heart’s desires, and who swiftly delivers one from the ocean of existence— should contemplate her.
Thus say the Śrutis.
Now, one should meditate upon the venerable Śrī Śaṅkara Bhagavatpāda.
Salutations to Śrī Nīlasāradā!

She blazes with a garland of flames, radiant and seated in the midst of a funeral pyre; she is well-nourished yet short of stature, standing while pressing a corpse with her left foot at its throat and crushing it with her right foot.
With a large, pendulous belly, she is beautiful with the expanse of full breasts like rain-clouds;
her three eyes are fixed upon the red Javā flower, and her face is terrifying with a lolling tongue and fangs.
Her limbs are covered with the skin of a black antelope, her face is graced with a gentle smile, and a blue lotus rests in the midst of her mass of matted hair.
Upon the region of her head shines a brilliant saffron-colored cloth, and in the center of her matted locks dwells the form of Akṣobhya.

With their heads bound together by hair, from which blood flowed as they were severed, they wore a garland of fifty human heads; their bodies were adorned with rows of heads cut off by the sword, numbering exactly fifty.
She who holds a great sword that flashes in her right hand while perpetually devouring human flesh,
and in her left hand she bears a blue lotus stalk slightly curved and shimmering with blood-red fibers.
In her right hand she holds aloft a white chisel, and in her left hand a skull-cup;
she is the embodiment of the universe, shattering the dullness born of worldly existence with the stroke of the chisel held in her hand. (6)

For she was adorned with a high, matted lock of hair bound with forest flowers, with earrings shimmering like the passion of a swift-moving elephant, with a radiant breast-ornament, and was made beautiful by the splendor of her great serpent-body and her throbbing, lovely armlets.
She was beautiful with shimmering blue and white serpent-bracelets gleaming on her arms like golden serpents,
and she wore upon her body a lovely sacred thread fashioned from the finest durvā grass and black serpents.
And she who holds a pure, beautiful *koṭeya* thread, white as a *kunda* flower, properly fashioned by the Naga;
and who, out of great greed for food, wears circular ornaments on both her feet, fashioned by the Naga. (9)
Bearing upon her forehead a terrifying skull-marked with a garland of various bones,
she who has long been the object of my contemplation— possessing such a beautiful form, peerless, faultless, inconceivable, and boundless— is here.

She whose feet are reddened by the luster of the bowstring of the Muraripu (Viṣṇu), who bestows the desired fruits upon those who have bowed down, and by whose grace one may attain the fame born of this entire universe—she rejoices eternally. (11)
Whoever should recite this praise of Sadaiva with a single-minded heart will certainly find a dwelling in this world;
he shall have neither poverty nor sin, nor shall he be of evil intellect, and desiring the Dharma, he shall likewise attain liberation. (12)
These various meditations on the unborn, matted-haired Lord (Śiva) and on the Goddess (Vidyā) are presented here for their beauty, as seen in their respective contexts.
Thus ends the "Various Meditations on the Goddess" composed by the venerable Śaṅkarācārya in the Bhujangaprayāta meter.
Having thus meditated upon the Self as being of such a nature, one performs the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi).

Then, having drawn a triangular, circular, and square mandala on one's left side, one should place a skull-cup or other vessel upon a support there; for as stated in the *Tantrarāja*: "In this regard, the skull-cup is clearly the producer of accomplishment," and so forth.

Having filled it with pure water using the root mantra, and having cast bilva leaves, red sandalwood, vajra-flowers, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and so forth, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) and other parts upon the face of the *arghya* vessel and in the cardinal directions; then—

Having recited the ten root-mantras (mūlavidyās), one should perform the *prāṇāyāma* and other rites after making the *arghya*— consisting of all mantras— into a form composed of light by means of water consecrated with that same recitation.
This is stated in the *Phetkāriṇī*:
Having performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), one should then proceed with the installation of the arghya vessel and other offerings;
thereafter, one should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) and carry out the ritual placement of the seers and other factors (ṛṣyādi-nyāsa).
Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon the hands and limbs, one should contemplate oneself as Anantāriṇī.
Then, reciting the root-mantra (*mūlavidyā*) four times through the left nostril, [one should inhale] through the left nostril.

Having offered [the breath] to Vāyu and having performed the recitation of that same [mantra] sixteen times, one should perform kumbhaka in the central channel and exhale through the right nostril by means of the eightfold victory of Bālā. This is for those who are unable [to do otherwise].
If one is able, one should perform [the ritual] with sixteen, sixty-four, or thirty-two [repetitions].

At the head: *Namaḥ to Akṣobhya, the ṛṣi*. At the mouth: *Namaḥ to Bṛhatī, the meter*. At the heart: *Namaḥ to Ekajaṭā, the deity*. At the seed-syllable *Hūṃ*: *Namaḥ*. At the secret place, having uttered the remainder: *Namaḥ to the Kīlaka*.
And likewise again: "The application [of this mantra] is for the sake of attaining my poetic skill, scholarship, and so forth. (Nīlatantra, p.
The seer of this [mantra] is Akṣobhya; its meter is Bṛhatī;
its truth is the Goddess Nīlasarasvatī, who is protected throughout the three worlds.

The seed-mantra *hūṃ* shall be the power (*śakti*) that bestows the fruits of the four aims of life. One should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) on the hands and limbs. For it is said: *hrāṃ*, salutation to her whose form is speech in its entirety; [this is for] the thumbs. *hrīṃ*, salutation to her whose form is unbroken speech; [this is for] the index fingers. *hūṃ*, salutation to her whose form is the speech of Brahman.

On the two middle fingers: *Hraiṃ* salutation to her whose form is the speech of Viṣṇu. On the two ring fingers: *Hrauṃ* salutation to her whose form is the speech of Rudra. On the two little fingers: *Hūḥ* salutation to her whose form is the speech of all [the deities]. (p. 20a)

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) on the palms and backs of the hands with the mantra *karatalapṛṣṭayoḥ*, [one proceeds] again: *Hrāṃ akhilavāgrūpiṇyai namaḥ*—on the two middle fingers (*madhyamayoḥ*). *Hṛdayāya namaḥ*—with the index, middle, and ring fingers (*tarjanī-madhyamā-anāmikābhiḥ*) at the heart (*hṛdaye*). *Hrīṃ akhaṇḍavāgrūpiṇyai namaḥ śirase svāhā*—with the index finger (*tarjanī*).
With the two middle fingers at the head: *Hūṃ*, salutation to the one whose form is the speech of Brahmā; *Vaṣaṭ* to the crest-lock (*śikhā*).
Thus, with the two thumbs at the crest-lock: *Hraiṃ*, to Vijaṭā, the weapon (*astra*), *Phaṭ*.
Thus, with the index and middle fingers, perform the binding of the ten directions with three upward-sweeping rays of light.

This is the ritual procedure. Having thus performed the placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) and formed the *brahmāñjali* gesture, one should remain for a moment in a state of non-difference from the Self.
One should meditate as follows: upon him who has struck down [the enemy] with his foot placed in the *pratyālīḍha* posture, and who has seized the terrible *aṭṭahāsa* laugh.
Praised by the sword, the bow, the trident, and the skull-cup, born from the seed-syllable *hūṃ*, short-statured, blue,
with a massive tawny mass of matted hair and fierce protruding fangs, having deposited the dullness [of ignorance] into the skull-cup,
she herself is Ugratārā, the *haṃ* of the three worlds.

Having meditated upon the Mātṛkās as a mass of flowers as red as the rays of the sun, mixed with sandalwood and *akṣata* offerings, and having [visualized] the blood-red *akṣata* grains held in their hands; then, from one's heart, [one should project] the splendor of the root mantra,
which is pure knowledge and consciousness.

Having led that [nectar] of mine through the sequence of piercing the six cakras until it reaches the Supreme Śiva situated within the pericarp of the thousand-petaled lotus at the crown of the head, and having come to rest in that ocean of nectar by means of repeated drawing-in, that nectar—

Having brought forth the overflowing stream of bliss through the nostrils, one should invoke it into the visualized form: "O Goddess, who are easily accessible through devotion, accompanied by your retinue,
remain perfectly steady for as long as I worship you."
"O Ekajaṭā, bring [them] here, bring [them] here!"—thus one should show [the gesture] by placing the añjali.
"Stay here, stay here!"—thus [one says] facing the *sayavādhyā*. "Be present here"—thus [one says]. With the thumb and fist, on page 21b:
"Be firmly restrained here. With the thumbs of all [fingers] and the fists. Then, upon the body, the sword (*khaḍga*).
One should perform the placement [of the mantra].

Having performed the consecration of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) with "Oṃ Āḥ Hrīḥ Kroḥ Hūṃ Svāhā," one should worship with the five offerings using the mantra: "Śrīmadekajaṭe vajrapuṣpaṃ pratīccha hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. Then...
One should display the *yonimudrā*. [To] the southeast: *hrāṃ*, homage to the Heart of Ekajaṭā.
To the northeast: then *aṃ a kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ*; thereafter, the best of practitioners should touch the right arm while uttering *ṅaṃ caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ ṭaṃ*.

Having assigned *ṭha*, *ḍa*, *ḍha*, and likewise *tathā* to the left arm, one should again assign *ṇa*, *ta*, *tha*, and *da*. Then, *dha*, *na*, *pa*, *pha*, *ba*, and *bha* are to be assigned to the right [arm].

One should place [the syllables] on the shanks: *maṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ kṣaṃ* on the left side. Having thus performed the pervasive placement (*vyāpya-pratinyāsa*), one should recite the root-mantra (*mūlavidyā*) seven times as a pervasive application (*saptadhā-vyāpaka*), by which one becomes composed of the Goddess (*devī-maya*).

Then, having meditated upon the previously mentioned *iṣṭa* (chosen deity), one should visualize the *mātṛkā-mantra* within a handful of flowers— consisting of auspicious grains (*akṣata*), vajra-flowers, and the like, mingled with the rays of the sun— and [conceive] the root mantra as consisting of pure gnosis and consciousness (*caitanya*) in the form of radiant energy (*tejomayī*). Through the process of piercing the six chakras (*ṣaṭcakra-bheda*), [this energy ascends] to the thousand-petaled lotus situated at the head.

Having caused the Supreme Śiva to enter within the lotus and, through the repetition of the action, having come to rest in that ocean of nectar, one should bring forth with the nostrils that [nectar] which has become merged with it— an "I" consisting of bliss and consciousness.
One should invoke [the deity] into the imagined form:
"O Goddess of gods, fragrant with devotion, accompanied by your retinue,
remain well-established for as long as I shall worship you."
"O Śrīmad-Ekajaṭā, come here, come here!"—thus, while placing the *añjali* mudrā, one should show [the deity]. "Stay here"—with the face turned downward;

"be present here"—thus, with the thumb and fist [mudrās]. "Be well-restrained here"—thus, with all [fingers] containing the thumbs within. Then, as with oneself, [one should perform the same] upon the body of the Goddess.

One should perform the placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga-vinyāsa*). Having established the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) with "ĀṂ HRĪṂ SVĀHĀ," [one recites] at the end of the root mantra: "O Śrīmad-Dekejaṭa, accept this vajra-flower! HŪṂ PHAṬ SVĀHĀ."
Thus, one should worship with these sixteen services, beginning with water for the feet (pādya).
As it is said in the Phetkāriṇītantra:
"Having invoked [the deity], established [them], and meditated upon them, one should indeed perform the worship."
"O glorious Eka-jaṭa, accept this vajra-flower. Thus it is said.
One should worship again with the root mantra ending in "priya" and accompanied by the *satāla* [sound].
In the *Nīlatantra*: "Having joined it with all the mantras, one should offer it to the deity."
In the absence of the vajra-flower, one shall partake of the fruit through mere recollection.
In the *Mahātantra*,
within the *Mantranīlasarasvatī*, [are described] the water for the feet, the water for the guest-offering, worship, food, bathing, garments, and ornaments.

Subsequently, one should employ the sixteen services in the worship: perfume, flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings, water for sipping, betel leaf, ritual adoration, hymns of praise, libations, and prostration.
Thus it is said in the *Phetkāriṇī*:
"One should worship the six limbs on the body of the Goddess or upon its filaments.
At this very time, one should worship the lineage of gurus for the Goddess, starting from the northwest and ending in the northeast. In the event of inability to do so:"
From the three gurus; or else, according to the measure of the sages.
As it is said in the Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi:
The illustrious Īśvara said:
O Mother, O Goddess, O Mahāmāyā, you who set in motion both bondage and liberation!
Now I desire to hear the unsurpassed lineage of the gurus.
The Goddess said:
The lineage of the gurus is indeed manifold due to the extensive weight of the mantras;
one should always worship it with fragrant flowers that are white and red.
Alternatively, there is worship with the five-fold offerings (pañcopacāra) consisting of perfumes, food offerings, and so forth. Among these, regarding flowers, it is as stated in the *Matsyasūkta*:
"One should always worship with fragrant flowers that are white or red."
And with auspicious flowers such as bilva and maruvaka, excluding tulasī.
"Especially with *udrā* flowers, consecrated with the *vajra* mantra;
one should offer every kind of flower with a mind endowed with devotion."
Alternatively, it is stated in the *Mantracūḍāmaṇi*:
"Having offered the *argha*, one should cause a hibiscus flower (*japāpuṣpa*) to be presented while reciting the mantra:
'O you who accept the vajra-flower,' accompanied by this term of address."
And the food offering (naivedya) should be as described in the Matsyasūkta:
"One should offer milk-rice (pāyasa) and rice mixed with sesame (kṛśara), combined with sugar and jaggery; likewise, one should present curd from a cow mixed with honey and other such items."
The wise knower of mantras should also offer excellent śāṃla fish, pāṭīna fish, and the flesh of the lizard, combined with honey.
Then, having displayed the *yoni-mudrā*, one should worship the retinue of the Command (*ājñā-pratyaya*) as follows:
in the center and in the directions— namely, in the southeast, south, southwest, northwest, and north.
Or, one should worship the six limbs upon the body of the Goddess.
Let there be a fixed rule for the directions starting with the East:
"The direction between the one to be worshipped and the worshipper is called the East by the wise;
that to its right is the South, and that to its left is considered the North."
The *pṛṣṭha* is declared to be the western [direction], and it should be worshipped everywhere with "hrāṃ akhilavāgrūpiṇyai hṛdayāyai namaḥ."
"Salutation to Eka-jaṭā;
svāhā to the head"— thus, O Vāmānasollasa, by this sequence,
the lineage of gurus will become absorbed into the God.
The path of the desired mantra is such that its sphere of accomplishment is free from obstacles;
this is the lineage-succession (saṃtati-krama) of gurus who have become disciples.
In that case, there is no doubt that both mantras and vidyās are fruitless for up to nineteen generations— or even for nine, seven, or three.
If a disciple does not know the lineages of his gurus, his own lineage will be destroyed;
therefore, one should understand that the auspicious and inauspicious nature of the guru-lineage is even more significant than one's own lineage.
The giver of the mantra, O Maheśvarī, should be known as superior even to Janaka;
therefore, O Pārvatī, Goddess of the Gods, listen briefly with diligence.
Listen, O Tārāguṇvakṣa, to those who bestow both seen and unseen fruits:
Ūrdhvakeśa, Vyomakeśa, Nīlakeśa, and Vṛṣadhvaja.
The divine stream burns the Siddhas; now hear from me truly about the streams of the Siddhas.
Vasiṣṭha, Kurmanātha, Mīnanātha, Maheśvara,
and Harinātha— listen as I describe the lineage of human gurus.
Tārāvatī, Bhānumatī, Jayāvidyā, Manoharī,
Mukhānanda, Parānanda, Pārijāta, and Kuleśvara.
Virūpākṣa and Bhairavī have spoken; Tāriṇī is the Kula, Siddhaugha, Āmānavaugha, Divyaugha, and Parameśvarī.
Akṣobhya, who bears the form of the three serpents upon the crown of all,
and Ānandanātha ending with Śabda— these gurus bestow all accomplishments.
Even women are proclaimed to be goddesses in the form of gurus;
or rather, in all the scriptures, gurus are indicated as being everything.
O Maheśvara, listen to the two crest-jewels of the lineage, the deities, and the preceptors;
and as for whichever groups of sages are traditionally remembered in connection with whichever mantras.

Those various [deities] are to be worshipped at the beginning of the ritual service; I have described this briefly for those who are unable [to perform elaborate rites], so that the worship of the Guru may be accomplished in a concise manner.
Likewise, it is stated in that very same place:
One should indeed worship the triad of gurus under the name of the "Known Guru," or else the tetrad; beyond that, one should not engage in verbal discussion.
Now, another method [is presented],
as it was stated in the *Tārārṇava*: "The determination of the gurus, beginning with the *parasādi* [and so forth], is as follows."
In the beginning, O Lord of Gods, you are everywhere the giver of mantras and the supreme guru;
you are indeed the higher-lower guru (parāpara-guru), while I am the self-existent parameṣṭhi-guru.
She is herself the embodiment of primordial nature within all mantras and vidyās;
she is the Guru, the Supreme Guru, and then the Higher-Lower Guru.
The *Parameṣṭhi* and likewise the *Guru*—these are declared to be the gurus. Thus ends the *Śrīguruniṛṇaya*.
"O Akṣobhyavajra, accept this flower! Hūṃ Phaṭ Svāhā!
This is stated in the *Phetkāriṇī*.
"Vajrapuṣpa pratīccha hūṃ phaṭ svāhā.
By means of this mantra, there is no doubt that the name, the thread, and the *bilva* fruit are all [accomplished].
With this mantra, one should worship all the members of the retinue according to the ritual.
Oṃ, Śaṃpāṇḍura, accept this vajra-flower! Hūṃ phaṭ svāhā! Oṃ, Padmanābha, accept this vajra-flower! Hūṃ phaṭ svāhā! Oṃ, Amitābha, accept this vajra-flower! Hūṃ phaṭ svāhā!
Oṃ māmaka vajra puṣpaṃ pratīccha hūṃ phaṭ svāhā | Oṃ māmaka vajra puṣpaṃ pratīccha hūṃ phaṭ svāhā | Oṃ pāṇḍava vajra puṣpaṃ pratīccha hūṃ phaṭ svāhā |
Oṃ tāre vajra puṣpaṃ pratīccha hūṃ phaṭ svāhā.
Thus [it is recited] during the four watches beginning with the east.
Oṃ padmāntaka vajra, accept this flower, hūṃ phaṭ svāhā! Oṃ yamāntaka vajra, accept this flower, hūṃ phaṭ svāhā! Oṃ vighnāntaka vajra, accept this flower, hūṃ phaṭ svāhā!
Oṃ narāntaka vajra puṣpaṃ pratīccha hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. As it is stated in the Phetkāriṇī-tantra:
"Oṃ Akṣobhya, one should worship Tāriṇī on the head with vajra-flowers and so forth."
Likewise, indeed, the Locana, Śaṅkha, Pāṇḍara, and Padmanābhaka [are to be worshipped].
The mantra-practitioner should worship Amitābha in the four directions beginning with the east; likewise, he should worship Nāma and Māmakī together with Pāṇḍaravāsinī.
In the four corners, beginning with Brahmā and the others, one should worship them in sequence with their respective mantras.
At the gates, starting from the east, [one should worship] Padmāntaka and Yamāntaka.
Having worshipped Vighnāntaka, one should worship Narakāntaka; thus, having completed the worship, one should perform the daily fire-oblation (*nityahoma*). As stated in the *Somatujagavallī*:
"A mantra is not perfected if it is not recited (*japta*), nor does it bestow power if it is not offered in sacrifice (*huta*)."
One does not obtain the desired object by worshipping [the deity alone]; therefore, one should practice the triad.
Through worship one obtains worship; through recitation, accomplishment is attained without a doubt;
and through the fire-ritual, one gains prosperity and all accomplishments.
Also in the Nīlatantra (p.
"I shall proclaim the perpetual fire-oblation by which one attains all goals."
Having properly performed the worship, the offering (bali) should be presented according to the ancient rule.
Then the excellent practitioner should perform the recitation and the libation (tarpaṇa), as well as the offering of bali and the Vaiśvadeva rites, and he should also honor the Brāhmaṇas.
Having brought the fire according to the prescribed rule, one should say "Homage, homage to the flesh-eaters";
then, having set aside the portion for the flesh-eaters, the wise man should prepare the fire.
Then, having uttered the root mantra, one should [place] the fire in a pit (kuṇḍa), or on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), or upon the ground or a grass mat, by means of the three Vyāhṛtis.
Having offered three oblations, one should then perform the worship of the six limbs;
thereafter, having invoked the Goddess with the sixteen-fold root mantra.
Having offered oblations and performed praise, one should release the drop (*bindu*) into the mandala.
Then, having fashioned a triangular, circular, and square mandala on one's left, one should worship it there with flowers.
Having placed the vessel filled with the prescribed offering materials and touched it with the thumb and ring finger,
recite three times: Oṃ hrīṃ ekajaṭāyai mahāyakṣādhipāyai upanītaṃ baliṃ gṛhṇa 2 gṛhṇāpaya 2 mama śāntiṃ kuru 2 paravidyām ākṛṣya kruṭ 2 chindha 2 hrīṃ svāhā.

Having recited [the mantra], one should offer the *bali* offering. One should perform the recitation (*japa*) according to one's capacity with the *rahasya-mālā*, whether aloud (*nigadena*), in a whisper (*upāṃśunā*), or mentally (*mānase*).
One should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight thousand times. Regarding the characteristics of recitation (*japa*), it is as stated in the *Vimalā-tantra*:
"Withdrawal of the mind, purity, silence, and constant reflection upon the mantra."
Freedom from distraction and irreproachability are the causes for the attainment of victory.
One should recite the mantra with the voice; this is known as *nigada*, which is accompanied by victory (*sajaya*).
Reciting the mantra slowly, one should move the lips only slightly.
That which is suitable for hearing is [the audible recitation]; whispered recitation is a hundredfold more effective; and mental recitation is a thousandfold.
Regarding the secret method of recitation:
one should visualize the pervasion of the seed-syllable as a star with the brilliance of ten million lightning flashes within the *mūlādhāra*, *svādhiṣṭhāna*, and *maṇipūraka* centers.
In the same way, [the syllable] *phaṭ* is in the heart;
thus it has been said.
One should meditate on the syllable *phaṭ* in the heart within the six-petaled lotus (*ṣaṭpadyā*). As it is stated in the *Nīlatantra*:
"I shall explain the meditation on the mantra; through recitation, omniscience arises.
O Maheśānī, by means of meditation on the mantra, the various classes of mantras are perfected."
One should contemplate the entire Vidyā, which possesses the brilliance of ten million suns and is embraced by the Mūla-cakra, extending from the mūlādhāra to the brahmarandhra.
One should visualize the nectar, resembling ten million suns and difficult for even yogis to attain,
or else shining like the full moon, upon the top of the *kūrca* [mantra].
Alternatively, having visualized the form of a lamp upon the tongue of all vidyās,
and having visualized the tongue itself as the form of a lamp by means of the mass of its radiance, one should recite [the mantra].
Thus it is said in the Phetkārīya: "By merely searching [the mantra] with the tongue, even one who is mute shall become a skilled poet."
Now follows the determination of the daily worship and recitation.
One should recite the mantra one thousand times, or perhaps a hundred times a day;
or one may recite the mantra twenty times, for less than that is not honored.
And therefore:
O You who guard the secret of secrets, accept this recitation performed by us;
O Goddess, may success be mine through Your grace while You remain present.
Thus, with water for the *arghya* offering, water, and flowers, one should offer the mantra-recitation (*japa*), which consists of light, into the left hand of the Goddess, saying: "Offer this!
This procedure should be performed at night by those who desire special fruits.
Thus it is said in the Phetkāriya:
"Whatever offerings, worship, and so forth are performed with diligence at night always reach a state of inexhaustibility through the grace of the goddess Tārā."
That which follows midnight for two muhūrtas is designated as the night (rātri),
and it is also proclaimed as the "dark" (niśā).
In the *Māyātantra* and in the *Candracūḍāmaṇi*:
"O God, how can a practitioner not become a Kaulika if he does not perform his exertion at night and does not worship the Śakti at night?"
Then, having performed a circumambulation and offered praise, one should prostrate with a full-body salutation (aṣṭāṅga-praṇāma).
[The manner of] praise is as follows:
Oṃ! O Goddess of terrible form and great roar, who causes the destruction of all enemies; O Giver of Boons, protect me, who have come to you for refuge, from my fears.
O Goddess worshipped by the Suras and Asuras, served by Siddhas and Gandharvas,
O Goddess who removes the sin of dullness, protect me who have come to you for refuge!
O Goddess who is endowed with a mass of matted locks, who resembles a flickering tongue, and who swiftly bestows nourishment—protect me! || 3 ||
Salutations to you in your gentle form, in your boar form, and in your fierce form;
salutations to you in your form as the Creator—protect me! || 4 ||
O You who are affectionate toward Your devotees, You destroy the dullness of the dull-witted;
O Goddess, remove my delusion and protect me! (5)
O Goddess whose nature is the syllable Hūṃ, who are fond of offerings and fire-oblations, homage to you!
O Ugratārā, homage to you; protect me! || 6 ||
