There the fruit of worship shall arise for a duration of seven days.
Having gone there on the fourteenth day, one obtains the fruit of worshiping the Yakṣas;
in that city, one becomes a woman or a beast—of this there is no doubt.
Thinking with single-minded devotion that there is no other god superior to him,
and having partaken of the *mādrakavya* offering, one becomes devoted to his lineage.
When the practitioner falls into agitation, my own agitation arises;
therefore, the wise and excellent hero should remain composed and endowed with enjoyment.
Through enjoyment one attains happiness; through enjoyment one achieves the welfare of the family;
whatever one gives, whatever one sleeps upon, whatever one does, and whatever one worships [all proceed from it].
Having meditated upon all that as being of the nature of the Kula, the wise one should thus conduct himself—
alone in a solitary place, such as a cremation ground, a mountain, or a forest.
One should wander joyfully and without fear in an empty house or on a riverbank;
for heroes, the time for recitation is praised at all times.
This should be performed in every land and at every sacred seat; of this there is no doubt—provided that the Brahmin is excellent and devoted to the materials of his lineage.
That which beautifies the family should be performed through meditation according to the prescribed rite;
the delightful station of the family is within the interior of the *aparā* flower.
That thread [of existence] consists of the bliss of all the gods and is of the nature of the Great Black (Mahākāla) family;
within the Hayāri flower, the Goddess herself is Sadāśiva.

Having taken a small amount of that [liquid] for the sake of pleasure, and having placed sandalwood or the red dye of saffron in the midst of the flowers, one should there [visualize] the essence of Śiva.
One should then effect a union with the power of Śiva; that is the realization of oneness. Having contemplated for a moment right there, one should then contemplate the Supreme Goddess.
Where there is Aparājitā, flowers, the javā flower, Bhairava,
the red and white karavīra, droṇa flowers, and bandhūka;
Wherever the sacrificial pit and the *mālatī* flower come to rest, there the Goddess shall dwell eternally; that place is my own place of worship.
If one offers a hibiscus flower and a silk cloth, one shall obtain the fruit [of one's desires];
the sin of killing a Brahmin and other such evils will certainly perish in an instant.
O Maheśvarī, it is indeed impossible to describe the majesty of Aparā;
however, the practice of vīrasādhana must be performed by heroic men.
It should be performed even by the gods, but not by beasts or commoners;
it is certain that the supreme heroic power belongs to the commoner, and not to the beast.
Whatever conventions and mantra-achievements were previously taught,
the hero of great power should perform them, including the ointment, the pill, and so forth.
The divine *bheda* exists through the hero; that which is called *bheda* is characterized by being peaceful, disciplined, sweet, and endowed with the grace of artistic skill.
A hero with an uplifted mind generally acts like a god;
he may be adorned with ornaments or even anointed with sandalwood paste.
Ākāra is Gopana, Vāpi, Yakovākula, and Bhairava; his limbs are smeared with red sandalwood paste, whether he be a Vaiṣṇava or a non-Vaiṣṇava.
Whether he be unconditioned like a mass of hair or conditioned as the Lord of the Family,
he should always remain joyful and contented in both dishonor and honor.
Whether intent on censuring the gods or even intent on their worship and so forth,
one who is devoted to worship there and established in the doctrine of the potter (Kulāla) is [a true practitioner].
Endowed with your own true nature, you shall dwell upon the earth like a god.
At the end of your lineage, the preliminary practice (puraścaryā) should be performed at night, or otherwise not so.
O Goddess, just as the twice-born who are devoid of the Vedas cannot be honored with mantras,
so too devotion does not flourish without devotion to Viṣṇu.
Just as knowledge of the Śakti leads to nothing but ridicule if it is devoid of liberation,
so too there is no entitlement whatsoever to the mantra without a Guru.
Just as a woman deprived of her husband is defeated in all her activities,
so too is a goddess without her clan, or my heroic practitioner.

One who belongs to the Kaula lineage is not qualified [if he lacks devotion]; therefore, one should be intent upon the inner state (bhāva). How can he whose family is undisciplined be a worshiper of me?
Therefore, one should act with such effort that one becomes adorned with discipline;
for in matters of existence and non-existence, there is no entitlement whatsoever to the family or the scripture.
By that, the practitioner who has purified his being becomes a Kaulika.
The venerable Goddess said:
I shall proclaim the state of the sacrificial animal (paśubhāva); listen with a well-concentrated mind.
Having received the initiation of the animal according to the rule, one should be intent upon that state.
First, for the sake of preliminary service, one should diligently practice purification;
one should eat fishless food and not even mentally recall women.
One should not harbor pride while enjoying wealth obtained through greed for another's property,
whether on the shore of the ocean, in a forest, on a mountain, or in a temple of the gods.
At the root of a bilva tree, in a secluded place, or in a beautiful sacred field, one should perform the *tūdra-darśana*; one must diligently abandon all crookedness.
The deity should be meditated upon in a state of purity by those who are well-composed.
There should be worship of the deity at the three junctions of the day, and one should perform recitation at the three junctions of the day.
One should never touch the rosary or the yantra at night;
one should not recite the mantra after eating, but should remain silent during all ritual acts.
The best of practitioners should never approach a woman at any time;
he should worship her with flowers, perfumes, water, and even while sleeping.
One should completely avoid sexual intercourse, talk about it, conversation regarding it, and social gatherings concerning it;
one should not approach [a woman] except during her fertile period, nor should one approach her with excessive passion.
One should have faith in listening to the Purāṇas and be devoted to the Vedas and the meaning of the Vedas;
one should not know [it as proper] to eat at night, nor [use] betel-leaf, O Supreme Lord.
Whatever has been commanded by the Guru, one should perform all of that with every effort;
even a mere flower [offered] therein is a cause for success, for Bhairava is present there.
Having touched a woman, one becomes pure after three nights by means of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
One who is devoted to the Goddess with supreme faith should not wear dyed clothing.
One should perform the rites prescribed in the Viṣṇu-mantras and so forth, as well as the ritual procedures;
however, one must never engage in talk concerning heroes or engage in their censure.
Devoted to that dharma, he performed the daily śrāddha, the offering of food to the Lord, the twilight worship (saṃdhyāvandana), bathing at sacred fords (tīrtha), and visiting the ten seats (pīṭhas).
O God, the animal sacrifice is of various kinds, along with Bhairava mentioned previously;
he has authority over this worship, but by no means over the office of a Guru.
One who has gone abroad has no authority over worship and other rites performed in his own country;
however, one who remains at home must perform them at all times outside [of his own territory].
By the mere sight of the former, one should perform the sight of the Kula; O Radiant One, even sins such as the killing of a Brahmin and the like are excelled by this teaching.
I choose only that which was seen before as the truth, the absolute truth;
for even my own self, O Lord of Gods, is but a manifestation of You, O Radiant One.
Nevertheless, a doubt arises in me at every step regarding that;
it would be better to abandon one's family than to bring harm upon one's own lineage.
Better is the reproach of one's own family, better is the bondage of one's own family,
better even the ruin of one's own family, and better the censure of one's own family.
It is better to bring ruin upon one's own family through body, mind, or speech;
one should not engage in a former sexual union for fear of the destruction of one's limbs.
In the mere family, there is a twofold evil:
the leader of the family is censured within his own kin, while the Lord of the Family is censured in the supreme ether.
Moreover, that evil arises from association with the vulgar;
therefore, in that regard, two states of being exist in every way, and they are not manifest in any manner whatsoever.
The bound soul (paśu) is proclaimed to be twofold: as existence (saṃbhāva) and as non-existence (vibhāva).
That [bound soul] is "existence" because it takes recourse in birth through the state of being a bound soul (paśubhāva), owing to its manifestation [in that condition].
From the heroic state one becomes divine, and from that, the divine is born;
from the divine a hero is born, and from the hero the divine is born.
Regarding the divine, there is no doubt that it is established as being equal;
however, since emotion (bhāva) is a property of the mind, how could it possibly exist in sound?
Therefore, existence must indeed be established; only a mere indication has been given here, just as the sweetness of sugarcane and jaggery is known by the teeth in the mouth.
In this way, O Lord, existence and non-existence are contemplated by the mind;
yet that which is the one great existence alone assumes manifold forms.

By means of the existence of various limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), the Lord— who is a mass of intense bliss and who assumes the form of primordial nature (*prakṛti*)— will bring about the differentiation of states of being.
That very Self is of the nature of rasa; He is considered the Lord, the Supreme.
He is to be heard, He is to be reflected upon, and He alone is to be meditated upon.
I declare that the Supreme Lord is to be directly realized through the flute;
O Goddess, by means of various states of being, one's own state is led to that very place.
Just as various kinds of food, once eaten, become a single taste through the process of digestion,
so too does one obtain manifold results from the Lord through the application of diverse means.
O God, from grass the sap is produced; from that comes the supreme sap;
from that arises the oblation, and from that, too, the emergence of the sap.
That very [cause] is the cause therein, yet that effect is not found;
and yet, O Mahādeva, neither effect nor cause is perceived.
In the very same way, this very self is born, is being born, and has been born within various bodies and wombs; it is perceived as such due to the distinctions of time.
Just as he was born and grew up, so too did he emerge again with his wife,
his male and female offspring, his neuter children, his learning, and his prosperity.
Through the application of various practices, the Lord assumes various forms;
yet He is that one Self alone, the eternal, whose nature is all forms.
That which is unmanifest becomes manifest; it is certainly known through its own nature (prakṛti).
Therefore, it is known through union with that nature, and never otherwise.
Just as a jar is not perceived when deprived of its connection with "jar-ness," so too an entity,
even while being distinguished from others, does not attain that distinction [if the defining property is absent].
Without me, no distinction whatsoever exists in the person;
it is not attained through ritual applications, nor through knowledges, nor by hearing the sequence of the gurus.
By its very nature, the self consists of knowledge, yet by its very nature, the person is obscured;
everything is presided over by Prakṛti, and the entire world is deceived by Prakṛti.
By its very nature it attains non-difference; by its very nature it dwells with all.
Neither the object, nor Prakṛti, nor the Puruṣa, nor even the Supreme Lord exists apart from that nature.
The knowledge of the equal flavor (*samarasa*) of those two is the reality of the thing, Maheśvara;
the union of both, however, is in truth the supreme state.
In this [state], the wise one knows for himself that this person is the very nature of consciousness;
he is the changeless God of all, the person who is beyond the range of the senses.
O Lord of Gods, the self-existent Self becomes manifest;
there are many means for this, as well as knowledge of the eternal Brahman.
Nevertheless, by means of yoga applied to the present subject, one shall quickly attain direct perception,
just as one who has boarded a boat reaches the shore while holding firmly to the helm.
Having crossed the ocean from various lands, he enters [the city] after a long time; in that same way, O Lord, they board this boat and cross over in an instant.
O Lord, one may attain Brahman through the power of Viṣṇu, and even by His grace;
yet if there is no distinctness therein, how can that [power] be the cause of its manifestation?
Therefore, those [subsequent factors] are born from what is further beyond them, for they have attained the status of causes;
they are not the causes of the entity itself, since the primary cause is primordial nature (prakṛti).
The female state is to be known as Prakṛti, while the Supreme Puruṣa is her power;
let Bhairaveśvara be understood through the distinction between the manifest and the differentiated.
Furthermore, its state as a jar is the cause of its differentiation from external objects;
likewise, through a modification of cognition, it has attained the state of being cognized even by another.
This very [state] is the direct cause, and by its very nature it is the Lord;
he in whose mind the divine state and the heroic state are established.
That very Self is liberated while living; for the sake of enjoyment, it attains the earth.
O son of the Goddess, that very Self is proclaimed as Bhairava.
"O Mahādeva, among the three states, two states are self-established; they are not to be spoken of, for they are the essence of Kula, the supreme Kula."
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Determination of the Elements," in the commentary on the *Śrītārārahasya*. 11.
Then, having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, for the sake of destroying all impurities within his own body,
[he should meditate on] the white-colored one with two arms, bestowing boons and fearlessness, situated upon the pericarp of a thousand-petaled lotus at the crown of the head.

Having visualized [the deity] adorned with white garlands and unguents, accompanied by the red-colored Śakti Vimalarūpiṇī who stands clearly to his left, and having worshipped him with mental offerings, one should recite "Aiṃ" as many times as possible.
Salutations to that venerable Guru by whom that state was revealed— the state which is of the nature of an unbroken circle and by which all that is moving and unmoving is pervaded.

Having thus praised and prostrated, one should visualize the root-mantra (*mūlavidyā*)— as pale-red as ten million rising suns— extending from the base (*mūla*) to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), and [repeat it] with intensive practice (*kriyāsamabhihāra*).
Having thoroughly wiped the thread with pure water and recited the root mantra as much as possible, one should rise, attend to necessary duties,
and go to a river or other suitable place for bathing, making the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "I shall perform this bath for the purpose of becoming fit for the worship of the Goddess."
Having bathed according to the prescribed procedure, one should commence the mantra-bath;
having immersed oneself three times while reciting the root-vidyā, one should rise up while reciting that same root-vidyā.
Having sprinkled water from a jar with joined palms over oneself three times with water consecrated by reciting [the mantra] three times,
one should perform the sipping of water (ācamana) three times with the root-vidyā, followed by the libations (tarpaṇa) for the gods, the ṛṣis, and the ancestors.

Having performed the rite with the root mantra at the end [of the recitation], having satiated the illustrious Ugratārā— Eka-jaṭā and Nīlasarasvatī— either twenty-five times, or fifteen or twenty-five times, or three times; then, rising from the water, putting on two washed garments, performing the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), and offering the arghya to the Sun in a vessel made of copper or similar material.

Having offered sandalwood paste, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), flowers, and white *aparājitā* blossoms, he should offer the water of honor (*arghya*) three times with the mantra: "To the one who dwells within the orb of the rising sun, who is eternally arisen as pure consciousness, to the glorious Śrī Eka-jaṭā, svāhā! Then, having visualized the Goddess in the center of that [mandala].
We know the one with a single matted lock; we meditate upon the Sole Heroine; may Tārā inspire us. We know the Sole Heroine; we meditate upon the Most Fierce One; may the Goddess inspire us.
Having thus recited the *ityetārā* Gāyatrī according to one's capacity, and having withdrawn [the deity] into the heart by means of the *saṃhāra-samudrā*, one then proceeds to the place of yoga.

"Oṃ vajrodake hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. Having thus consecrated the water with this water-mantra, and having set this water aside for the purpose of all ritual services, one should pour a little of it into other water. With that same water, reciting the mantra "Oṃ hrīḥ svāhā," one should wash one's feet while holding *kuśa* grass in the hand.
p.
135b) Having placed gold and silver coins from various families into the right hand as they appear, and having held those gold and silver coins in the ring finger of the family’s auspicious hand—
Oṃ hrīṃ viśuddhadharma gāyatrī sarvapāpāni śamaya pāleṣa vikalpātayana hūṃ phaṭ svāhā.
Having sipped water according to the ritual rule, one should visualize the seat there; having visualized the cremation ground there, [one should meditate] therein.
One should meditate upon the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpadruma).
At its base is a jeweled pedestal adorned with various gems,
decorated with diverse ornaments and the like, and graced by sages and deities.
Then,
in the four directions, there were auspicious *cāmuṇḍās*, rejoicing with abundant flesh and bones, adorned with funeral pyre embers and skeletal remains.
In the midst of that, one should visualize the Goddess according to the prescribed method of meditative yoga.
Having meditated, [one performs] the binding of the topknot with: *oṃ maṇidharī vajriṇi sarvaśaṃkari hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*.

Oṃ rakṣa 2 hūṃ phaṭ svāhā! One should purify the ground with the sprinkling of water. With the mantra "Oṃ sarvavighnān sāraya hūṃ phaṭ svāhā," one should scatter unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) using the *nārāca* and *sūdra* mudrās, thereby dispelling the three kinds of obstacles.
Oṃ pavitra vajrabhūme hūṃ phaṭ svāhā.
Having consecrated the ground with this, then [prepare] a seat such as a soft woolen rug (*kambala*) or a grass mat (*viṣṭara*), as appropriate.

Having spread out the common [offerings], there, with the mantra *oṃ āḥ surekhe vajrarekhe hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*, one should worship it with red scents and flowers and sit down in the sequence beginning with the svastika. Then, with this mantra, [one should draw] a maṇḍala on the ground.
Having reflected thus, one should take one's place upon that seat and then sit down. Some say: "Even on the seat," while others say:
"Oṃ maṇidhari vajriṇi mahāpratisare rakṣa 2 hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. (p. 137a)

One should tie a protective knot at the edge of the garment. With "Oṃ Āḥ Hūṃ Phaṭ Svāhā," one performs the purification of body, speech, and mind through pervasive [recitation]. Oṃ, homage to the Tathāgata, the Perfectly Awakened One, the King named Puṣpaketu; Oṃ Puṣpe Puṣpe Mahāpuṣpe Supuṣpe Bhūṣite, and to that which is strewn with flowers.

Having consecrated the flowers and other offerings with the mantra *hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*, one should draw the maṇḍala upon a pedestal made of gold or other materials, which has been smeared with red sandalwood, *gorocanā*, saffron, and *vajrapuṣpa* powder, using the mantra:
*bhuṃ āṃ surekhe vajrarekhe hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
Just as there is an eight-petaled lotus enclosed within a triangle, consisting of four gates:
at the tip of the triangle is *hrīṃ*, in the south *trīṃ*, in the north *phaṭ*, in the west [at the tip of the triangle], and in the center of the triangle *hūṃ*.
One should write the sādhya [name] together with "Make my swift poetic skill, *kuru kuru*," and so forth.

Having placed red sandalwood, gambhārī, and other materials upon a pedestal (pīṭha) in front of this yantra, one should worship the pedestal as follows: in the center, from top to bottom, "Salutation to the cremation ground (*śmaśāna*); salutation to the wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpavṛkṣa*); salutation to the pedestal at its base."
Homage! Homage to the various jewels! Homage to the various ornaments! Homage to the sages! Homage to the gods! Homage to the jackals, who rejoice in much flesh and bone!
Salutation to the corpses in the four directions. Salutation to Muṇḍa. Salutation to Citāṅgāra. Salutation to Asthi.
Then, in the eight petals, starting from the direction of the deity [the east] in sequence: Oṃ, salutation to Lakṣmī. Oṃ, salutation to Sarasvatī.
Oṃ, salutation to Rati. Oṃ, salutation to Prīti. Oṃ, salutation to Kīrti. Oṃ, salutation to Śānti. Oṃ...
Homage to Puṣṭi! Oṃ, homage to Tuṣṭi!
In the center, [homage] to Hmau Mahāpretāsana! Having thus worshipped, upon that— (p.

With the root mantra, one should perform the visualization of the form and the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*). Just as in the sequence of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), having meditated on the syllable *hrīṃ* of red color at the navel, one should disperse the ashes with the wind arising from it.
Then, having visualized the white-colored syllable *hūṃ* at the head, one should [disperse] those bones with the wind arising from it.
Having caused the entire form of the cremation ground to be flooded, one should flood the entire universe in the form of the body.
One should meditate upon the stainless Tāriṇī, whose nature consists of the self, who has reached the end of expenditure, and whose essence is the goal.
Likewise, within that nectar-water which pervades the universe and takes the form of the cremation ground...
Having meditated on the syllable *ĀḤ* as a red flower, and having visualized a white lotus arising from the syllable *ṬAṂ* above it,
one should meditate on the syllable *HŪṂ*, resembling the color of a sapphire, above that; [and then] a knife adorned with the seed-syllable *HŪṂ*.
One should meditate; one should meditate on [the deity] situated above the agent. Having meditated upon oneself as Tāriṇī...
Standing in the pratyālīḍha posture, she is Aghorā, adorned with a garland of severed heads,
short-statured, pot-bellied, terrifying, and clad in a tiger-skin garment.
Endowed with fresh youth, adorned with the five mudrās,
four-armed, with a protruding tongue, she bestows the boon of great flesh.
Her two right and left arms are joined with a sword and a knife,
and her pair of right hands are endowed with a skull-cup and a lotus.
One should meditate on her with a single tawny and fierce matted lock, adorned with a garland of skulls upon her head;
having thus performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), one should proceed with the ritual placement of the offering water (argha).

Just as one should prepare a mandala consisting of a triangle, a circle, and a square on one's left, place there a vessel such as a skull-cup with eight supports, fill it with pure mercury using the root mantra, cast bilva leaves, red sandalwood, vajra-flowers, and unbroken rice grains into it, and [arrange offerings] in the southeast, northeast, southwest, northwest, in the center, and in the cardinal directions.
The days: *Oṃ hrāṃ*, homage to the heart; *Oṃ hrīṃ*, *svāhā* to the head;
*Oṃ hūṃ*, *vaṣaṭ* to the crest-lock; *Oṃ hraiṃ*, *hūṃ* to the armor; *Oṃ hrauṃ*, to the three eyes.

Vauṣaṭ! Oṃ hṛ astra-aya phaṭ! Having performed the placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) and having recited the root-mantra ten times, and having made [the deity] consist of all vidyās by means of a threatening gesture full of splendor—thus having prepared the arghya and performed breath-control (prāṇāyāma) and so forth.

Just as one should recite the root-mantra ten times, one should fill the air through the left nostril and recite that same mantra sixteen times; having drawn it up through the *suṣumnā* channel, one should recite this very mantra eight times and exhale the air through the [right] nostril which was previously observed.
Having thus performed *prāṇāyāma* according to one's capacity, one should deposit [the mantras] with *hūṣya* and so forth:
"Homage to Akṣobhya, the *ṛṣi*, on the head; on the mouth..."
Salutation to the *Vṛhatī* meter; to the heart. Salutation to the deities of the single-crested (*eka-jaṭā*); to the *mūlādhāra*.
Salutation to the seed-syllable *hrīṃ*; to the heart. Salutation to the power (*śakti*) of *phaṭ*. Having recited the remaining syllables, salutation to the *kīlaka* for all limbs.

Furthermore, for the very same purpose as before—namely, for the attainment of my swift poetic skill and scholarship—there is this application. One should perform the ritual assignment (*nyāsa*) of the hands and limbs. Likewise:
*Hrīṃ*, salutation to Ekajaṭā with the two thumbs; *hrīṃ*, salutation to Tāriṇī with the two index fingers;
*hūṃ*, salutation to Vajrodakā with the two middle fingers;
*hraḥ*, salutation to Ugrajaṭā with the two ring fingers; *hrauṃ*, salutation to Mahāparisara with the two little fingers.

*Namaḥ* to the two little fingers; [to] the two little fingers. *Hraḥ*, O Piṅgogra Eka-jaṭā, *namaḥ* to the palms and backs of the hands; [to] the palms and backs of the hands. Thus is the Karaṅga-nyāsa.
Now, the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*).

*Hraiṃ*, obeisance to the heart of Ekajaṭā; thus, with the index, middle, and ring fingers, at the heart. *Hrīṃ*, *svāhā* to the head of Tāriṇī; with the index and middle fingers. *Hūṃ*, to the crest-lock of Vajrodakā.

"Vaṣaṭ"—thus, at the crown of the head with the pair of thumbs below. "Haṃ, O fierce one with matted hair, to the armor, Huṃ"—thus, with both hands from the head down to the feet. "Hrauṃ, to the three eyes of the Great Perimeter, Vauṣaṭ"—thus, with the index, middle, and ring fingers, [placing them] on the three eyes. "Hraḥ, Piṅga-ugra-eka... [to the third eye].
*Vāgrupiṇyai kavacāya hūṃ*—thus, with both hands, [one should touch] from the head down to the feet. *Hrauṃ rudravāgrūpiṇyai netratrayāya vauṣaṭ*.

Thus, with the index and ring fingers, [one touches] the three eyes. With "Hraḥ, to the weapon for her whose form is all speech, Phaṭ," one should perform the binding of the ten directions with three upward claps and *chotikās* using the index and middle fingers.
This has been stated in the *Siddhasārasvata*:
Having uttered "akhilā-vāgrūpiṇī," one should say "namas" for the heart;
"akhilā-vāgrūpiṇī" [followed by] "śirase svāhā" (the beloved of Agni);
and having uttered "brahmā-vāgrūpiṇī," one should also say "śikhāyai vaṣaṭ."
Having uttered "Viṣṇavāgrūpiṇī," one should recite "huṃ" for the armor (kavaca).
Having uttered "Rudravāgrūpiṇī," one should say "vauṣaṭ" for the three eyes (netratraya).

One should remember: "Sarvavāgrūpiṇī śaktā astrāya phaṭ. One should practice the six long vowels and join them at the end of the *māyā* seed-syllable (*hrīm*). Alternatively, it is stated in the *Tantracūḍāmaṇi*:
At the end of the seed-syllable, the heart mantra is proclaimed for Ekajaṭā;
likewise, for Tāriṇī it is on the head, and similarly for Vṛjodakā it is on the crest-lock (śikhā).
For Ugrajaṭā, it is the armor (kavaca), and likewise for Mahāparirasa.
Likewise, his eyes are proclaimed to be tawny and fierce, with a single matted lock (*jaṭā*).
Thus, the placement of the seat (*pīṭhanyāsa*) and the placement of the phonemes (*varṇanyāsa*) have been described, because they are endowed with the form of the *Tārā* mantra.
This has been stated in the *Phetkāriṇī*:

"One should perform the placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) and the hands (*karanyāsa*) here alone; one should practice what is taught here in this [system]. Perform the placement (*nyāsa*) as it is joined [here];
one should not perform a placement taught in another tantra. Furthermore, regarding the placement of the phonemes (*varṇanyāsa*), it is stated in the *Kālikātantra*:
One should practice the phonemes of the *mātṛkā* as taught in the *Kālikātantra*. It is as follows:
"I shall proclaim the placement (*nyāsa*) of the phonemes, by which one becomes identical with the Goddess.
AṂ ĀṂ IṂ ĪṂ UṂ ŪṂ ṜṂ Ṝ̄Ṃ EṂ AIṂ OṂ AUṂ AṂ AḤ. Thus ends the section on the vowels.

Hraṃ! To the crest-lock (śikhā) in the water of the mouth, vaṣaṭ; in the northwest. Hraiṃ!
To the armor (kavaca) of the fierce matted-hair one, huṃ; in the pericarp. Hrauṃ! To the three eyes of the great circumference, vauṣaṭ; in the four directions.
HRA PIṄGOGRAIKAJAṬE ASTRĀYA PHAṬ. Then, upon the crown of the Goddess:
AKṢOBHYA VAJRAPUṢPAṂ PRATĪCHA HŪṂ PHAṬ SVĀHĀ.
Having thus worshipped [the goddess], [one should worship] from the northwest (vāyavya) up to the northeast (īśa).
One should worship the power in the form of the Guru:
*Uṃ*! *Urdhvakeśānandanātha*, accept this vajra-flower, *Hūṃ Phaṭ Svāhā*.
Oṃ Vyomakeśānandanātha Vajra... and so forth. Oṃ Nīlakeśānandanātha Vajra... and so forth. Vṛṣadhvajānandanātha Vajrapuṣpa... and so forth. These are the Divine Lineage (divyaugha). || 1 ||
Oṃ Vasiṣṭhānandanātha Vajra, and so forth. Oṃ Harināthānandanātha Vajra, and so forth. Oṃ Jayāsu Vajra, and so forth.
Oṃ, Vijayādyasu, proceed, and so forth. Oṃ, Mahodarpasu, proceed, and so forth. Oṃ, Śākhānandanātha, proceed, and so forth.
Oṃ Parānandanātha, proceed, and so forth. Oṃ Yanānandanātha, proceed, and so forth. Oṃ Kulānandanātha, proceed, and so forth.
Oṃ virūpākṣānandanātha vajrapuṣpaṃ pratīccha hūṃ phaṭ svāhā | These are the multitudes of human beings.
If one is unable to do this, one should worship only Akṣobhya and the Goddess in these two [places].
Then, following the counter-clockwise direction (vāmāvarta), one should worship in the petals starting from the east.
Oṃ vairocana vajrapuṣpaṃ pratīccha hūṃ phaṭ svāhā | Oṃ śaṅkhapāṇḍala vajrapuṣpaṃ pratīccha hūṃ phaṭ svāhā ||
Oṃ padmanābha vajra puṣpaṃ pratīccha hūṃ phaṭ svāhā | Oṃ japa-puṣpam, and so forth. Then, by turning counter-clockwise, [offer] to the petals in the directions beginning with the southeast (Agni).
Oṃ, Nānāmakeśvara, go forth, and so on; Oṃ, Yamātta, go forth, and so on; Oṃ, Vighnāntaka, go forth, and so on; Oṃ Naṃ, Narakāntaka, go forth, and so on.
Having thus [dismissed] them with perfumes and other offerings, one should again worship the Goddess with perfumes and other offerings.
Having drawn a square mandala within a triangle situated to one's left.
Oṃ, having worshipped thoroughly with flowers, and having placed there the vessel containing the three-fold oblation (vali) as prescribed, and having touched it with the *tattva* and *āram* mantras:
Oṃ jrī! O Ekajaṭā, O Mahādhīmatī, accept this oblation brought by me; accept it, cause it to be accepted for my sake!
Bestow peace, bestow peace! Having drawn forth the supreme vidyā, pierce it, pierce it! Bring all the world under control! Hrīṃ svāhā!

Having thus recited [the mantra] and offered the *bali* with the secret rosary (*rahasyamālā*), one should recite the root mantra one hundred thousand times on that day for the sake of service; this is what is called the "secret name" (*guhyasaṃjñā*). One should then recite the root mantra one hundred times immediately thereafter.

In that regard, the secret of recitation (*japa*) is as follows: one should perform the practice after meditating upon the three seed-syllables (*bīja*) pervading the *mūlādhāra*, *svādhiṣṭhāna*, and *maṇipūraka* respectively—blazing like ten million flashes of lightning, mutually interwoven and inseparable, and purified of all [ordinary] radiance—and then contemplating the sound *phaṭ* as the form of ultimate rest. One should then proceed.
That mantra should be recited neither too slowly nor too quickly; thus, having recited it according to one's ability,
one should take the water for the *argha* offering and flowers, and [offer] that recitation which consists of radiant light.
O Great Goddess, you who guard that which is more secret than the secret itself, accept us, your people; O Sovereign Lady, may success be mine through your grace.

Having thus offered the recitation into the left hand of the Goddess, having meditated upon it as being made thin [subtle], and having praised her, one should prostrate with the eight-limbed salutation (*aṣṭāṅga-pāta*). Then, one should offer oneself to my supreme deity. Knowing "Oṃ tat sat," one should offer [oneself].

Oṃ tat sat. Having understood this, having performed the act of offering, and having displayed the *yoni-mudrā*, one should dissolve all the deities of the obstructions into one's own body; then, by means of the *saṃhāra-mudrā*, [one should absorb] the supreme splendor into one's own heart.

Having performed breath control (prāṇāyāma) and the six-limbed yoga (ṣaḍaṅga), one should offer the remnants of all [the offerings] to Nirmālavāsinyai, saying "Aiṁ! Salutation to Nirmālavāsinyai," and recite the remaining portion. One should give [the remainder] to those who remain. Having offered the lion [portion] to the seventy-seven [deities], one may dwell at ease; this is the daily worship (nityapūjā). This applies specifically to the preparatory rite (puraścaryā).
Having worshipped thoroughly.

Having recited the mantra one hundred thousand times, and having performed the fire sacrifice according to the prescribed rite in a four-cornered pavilion that has been consecrated for the first time, using white lotuses or bilva leaves as the oblation in a quantity equal to one-tenth of the recitation, [one should offer] black aloe-wood...
One should satisfy [the deity] with pure fragrant waters mixed with the three spices (vyoṣa) in one-tenth that amount;

then, with pure water in one-tenth of that amount, one should consecrate one's own head according to the instruction; and in one-tenth of that amount, one should [satisfy] a Brāhmaṇa or an excellent young girl.

One should satisfy the preceptor according to the prescribed rite with the milk, meat, and so forth of a woman, along with ghee, sugar-candy, and other offerings; then one should present the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the *Śrītārārahasyavṛtti*. 12.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the procedure for the fire-oblation (*homa*). Herein, the occasional (*naimittika*) rites and others follow the daily (*nitya*) ones, beginning with the *dīkṣā*. For the oblation, one should fashion a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) made of sand and other materials, elevated to the height of the hand or higher, according to my [tradition].
As it has been said: because worship consists of recitation (*japa*), fire-offerings (*homa*), and so forth, the characteristics of the image (*mūrti*) are [described] therein.

In that context, when the fire-offerings numbering a thousand or more have been performed and the bed and other items have been purified, [the ritual is performed] in a pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) measuring five or seven cubits on all sides.
One should construct an auspicious pavilion with four corners.
For the purpose of building that pavilion, one should do so to the east, north, or northeast of the Anuvāstu fire.
This has been stated in the Gaṇeśavimarṣiṇī:
Having taken possession of the site, the practitioner of mantra should, in the east, the northeast,
or the north, designate the mandala upon the ground according to its divisions.
It should be nine cubits in measure, or seven cubits,
or five cubits for a man; it should be square and well-proportioned.
One should construct a four-gated structure adorned with altars and archways,
surrounded by a fringe of *darbha* grass and encircled by a thread.
Regarding the position of a single sacrificial pit (*ekakuṇḍī*): a house measuring five cubits is indeed recommended. As it is stated in the *Homanirūpa*:
"Even according to the opinion of those who maintain a single pit, the house should be five cubits;
that [house] should have a square pit whose northern side is auspicious."
Thus it is stated in the *Gaṇeśavimarṣiṇī*:
"Likewise, in the north, one should construct a single quadrangular (*vedāsra*) pit;
for a *lakṣa-homa*, however, one should perform that in the center of the house."
"And some Tantrikas desire it to be square for all [deities]," thus it is stated in the *Sāradātilaka*.
O Great Goddess, one should accomplish all ritual purposes within a square; having condensed [the space] to the measure of four cubits, one draws it by contracting [the lines].
In that regard, the rule concerning the cubit for constructing a house or a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) is as follows:

The measurement of the middle finger of the right hand of the agent—that is, the sacrificer—is used to determine the [length of the] name-finger (nāmāṅgulī). This has been stated in the Vijñānīteśvara (p.
Just as there is a fixed rule regarding the number of cubits for constructing a house or a sacrificial pit,
so too must this be performed by the patron (yajamāna) himself and never by anyone else.
Now, "one finger-breadth (aṅgula) by eight [units]" means as follows. It is stated in the *Nīteśvara*:
"That which is a barley-corn (yava) in its [the finger's] measure is declared to be eight barley-corns;
a sesame seed (tila), however, is five-sixths of a barley-corn, and likewise one-seventh of a sesame seed."
One should fashion a three-year-old calf's tail; its length is six [units], or it may even be entirely according to what has been seen by those skilled in the auspicious measurements.
That measurement for the middle joint is twenty [units] beyond that.
By recollecting the traditional scriptures, fire is kindled by those who gather the fuel.
By that same measurement of finger-breadths (aṅgula), the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) should also be constructed.
Among them, the four-cornered pit is as follows:
One should mark the center according to the measurement of the original thread; that middle point is pure in both parts, and the same applies to the two ends.
O Matsya, one should form a pair of directions; then, within the belly of that fish, one should again lay down a thread of the proper measurement from south to north.

Having fixed those [threads] at the tips of the lines, one should draw all the squares within those grids; then, starting from the tip of the crocodile situated in the corner, one should cast threads toward the cardinal directions.
When this is done, a small square enclosure is produced;
this very thing shall be the quadrangular sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), possessing excellent characteristics.
And the measurement of the width of the pit, as well as its length, should likewise be the same.
One should fashion the girdle of that same measure, and the silver belt should be of the same kind;
it may consist of a single strand, or likewise a second one.
The width of the covering for the Vedādi-nayana is one cubit;
its inner covering is nine finger-breadths wide, while the [outer] covering is four finger-breadths wide.
In the *Kriyāsāra* as well, it is recorded that the primary girdle (*mekhalā*) is nine finger-breadths wide,
and the girdle outside of that is known to have a thickness of five finger-breadths.
Your girdle consists of three parts; it should be cut by two finger-breadths in sequence,
measuring four, three, and two *tulās* respectively, with the girdle itself being three [parts].
In every case, the field should be of this kind according to the proportions of the fire-pits (kuṇḍas);
likewise, leaving one finger-breadth (aṅgula), there shall be a girdle (mekhalā) within the pit.
In the case of a pit measuring one cubit, one should increase it in other pits;
the knower of mantras should construct each subsequent pit by increasing it by half a finger-breadth.
The first girdle is declared to be sāttvika, the second rājasa, and the third tāmasa; such is the determination regarding the girdles.
p. 151a) Now, the determination of the *yoni*:
first, there is the *mekhalā-yoni*; the *mekhalā* is in front of the *hotṛ*.
One who knows all the characteristics of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should fashion it with the color of a young elephant's trunk.
The *yoni* in a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) measuring one cubit (*hasta*) is said by the wise to be six *aṅgulas* in length, four *aṅgulas* in width,
and two *aṅgulas* in height.
A wise person should fashion the navel in the center of the pit (kuṇḍa) like an eight-petalled lotus,
or the learned one may fashion the navel there according to the specific requirements of each respective pit.
In this case, the depth and width of the navel should be four finger-breadths (aṅgulas);
however, in a pit measured by a fist or a cubit, the navel should be only four finger-breadths.

In the three sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) measuring two cubits [in width], one should gradually connect the *yoni* [to the base] by the measure of one finger-width each; likewise, one should increase the size of the navel (*nābhi*) accordingly.
The ground outside the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is prescribed as the "platform" (sthalam). In the center of this square area, one should construct a structure with an opening at its core.
With a thick base and a fine tip, its spokes being most beautiful,
one should cause it to be made starting from the position of the girdle located on the exterior.
This has been stated by Bhāskarācārya: "In the womb, at the stalk, it is perforated.

One should fashion a cavity (vila) in the middle of the womb; that is known as "the grasper" (agrāhi).
This has been stated in the *Gaṇeśavimarṣiṇī*:
"One should know the form of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) to be the supreme body of Prakṛti."
They say the belly is the sacrificial pit, and both hands are traditionally known as the two sides.
The two feet are in the fifth corner, like the moon upon the king of mountains;
the womb (yoni) is the cause of the hand, and its position is great.

Therefore, because the ritual procedures for the sacrificial offerings (havya) therein consist of that very essence, this [altar] is complete in its parts. The wise man should increase the height of the altar by one-eighth, and likewise make the navel circular;
or the best of practitioners should fashion it in accordance with the specific requirements of each particular fire-pit (kuṇḍa).
In the womb-pit (yonikuṇḍa), one should likewise fashion a lotus-womb;
from one hundred up to nine hundred [times], one should offer handfuls into the pit as a fire-oblation (homa).
In a field of one cubit, the yield is one thousand; in two cubits, it is remembered as ten thousand;
in four cubits, it is one hundred thousand; and in six cubits, it is one million.
In the case of an oblation, the limit is ten cubits; indeed, even for a Prācīna offering, it is ten. Beyond ten cubits, there is no sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) for a homa on this earth.
In that regard, the girdle (*mekhalā*) in a fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) measuring two cubits and so forth is as follows. It is stated in the *Sāradātilaka*:
"In a fire-pit of two cubits, O Vasudeva, [the girdles] should be known as four, three, and two [cubits].
In a sacrificial pit measuring four cubits, however, there should be four, three, and two finger-breadths [for the respective parts].
The pits (kuṇḍas) should have bases of ten, eight, or four finger-breadths (aṅgulas).
In a pit measuring eight cubits (vasuhasta), the lines are twelve finger-breadths;
in a pit measuring ten cubits, they are fourteen finger-breadths.
The wise should know that the girdle (*mekhalā*) is equal in length and height on all sides.
Now, the measurements for sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) of two cubits and so forth are as stated in the *Yāmalatantra*.
A man with one hand is prescribed for those with two sacrificial pits;
this was stated by the moon-crested Lord [Śiva] himself regarding the six-faced [Kumāra].
Listen now to the measurements for the mace, starting from one cubit and two cubits and so forth:
the cord [for measurement] is thirty-three finger-breadths long, augmented by twelve sesame seeds.
In a pit two cubits in size, one should arrange [the measurements] according to rule as before;
in a three-cubit [pit], it is forty *tilas* less than twelve corners.

In a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) of four cubits (*hasta*), one should proceed with fifty-three finger-breadths (*aṅgula*). Understand that by that same measure, the cord (*sūtra*) for a five-cubit [pit] is twelve [finger-breadths].
A cord of sixty-four finger-breadths increased by twelve sesamum-seeds,
and a cord of eighty-eight finger-breadths increased by twelve sesamum-seeds.
In a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) measuring seven cubits, one should indeed know how to abandon the thread;
the thread is nine and seven finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) long, marked with two, nine, and twelve [units].

In the case of a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) measuring nine cubits, the thread for those who know the ritual threads is considered to be one hundred and sixteen finger-breadths (aṅgulas), consisting of nine [units] joined with twelve.
In that case, for a pit (*kuṇḍa*) of ten cubits, the measurement is determined by extraction (*uddhāra*).
Here is the distinction:
here, in a pit of two cubits and so forth, the standard (*prakṛta*) cubit applies to the girdles (*mekhalā*), the womb (*yoni*), and other parts.
The increase is by two finger-breadths for every twenty-fourth part; that is the measure for the width of the *toraṇa* arch.
This is stated in the *Bṛhadyoginīhṛdaya*: "In sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) of two cubits and so forth, whatever the *vyomasūtra* may be...
By means of twenty-four movements, there is the measurement of various finger-breadths;
by that measure of finger-breadths, [the dimensions] are established in all directions for all fire-pits.
The conceptualization of the girdle, the womb, the neck, and so forth has been fully described.
Having thus understood the measurement in all cases, one should construct the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
An example of the fault of ignorance is as Viśvakarman said:
"If the excavation is excessive, there will be disease; if deficient, the loss of cattle and wealth;
if the altar (kuṇḍa) lacks its proper form, there is the destruction of progeny; and if the girdle (mekhalā) is broken, death [results]."
A sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) lacking a girdle is indeed called sorrow;
one deprived of its upper portion is said to cause the destruction of offspring; and that which is devoid of a neck is declared to be a defect.
Elsewhere, in the *Śrībhairava-ṣoḍaśa-sūtrādhika*, it is also stated: "In a site where there is division among friends, fear of pride, poverty, combat,
or a deficiency in the neck [of the ground], there will be no success in a root-digging."
If it is excessive, there is loss of wealth; if deficient, suffering arises.
Diseases arise, and there will be loss of wealth and food;
if the anus is cracked, perforated, or congested, death shall occur.
Thus, having understood this, one should indeed construct the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa). This is stated in the Rudrayāmala:
"Thus, O Goddess, the measurement for the sacrificial pits has been shown in brief;
it is seen in the Yoginīhṛdaya and spoken as the certain conclusion of the sages."

Having prostrated before the Guru and understood [the requirements], one should perform the construction of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) with devotion for the sake of benefiting the world through divine means.

Now, I shall describe the fire-ritual (*agni-kārya*): to the north of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), the practitioner of mantra should perform the fire-rite— whether it be daily, occasional, or for a specific desire—

in pits or on altars (*sthaṇḍila*) that have been prepared in various shapes such as squares and so forth, according to the requirements of those respective rites and in accordance with the measurements of the homa, as characterized by the scriptures.
In that regard, one should fashion the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) with eighteen ritual preparations (saṃskāra).
This has been stated in the *Lakṣadeśika-tantra*:
Therein, eighteen purificatory rites for the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) are prescribed:
sprinkling with the root mantra and cleansing with the arrow mantra.
Anointing with unguents, the visualization of the form of the digit (kalā), and immediately thereafter the drawing of the three lines; following this, worship with the heart-mantra is prescribed.

One should perform the vajrīkaraṇa (hardening) with the Astra-mantra, the purification with the Hṛdaya-mantra using auspicious kuśa grass, the sprinkling at the crossroads with the Tanūtra-mantra, and the removal of obstacles with the Tāra-mantra.
In Yoga, one should fashion a Kuṇḍalinī by means of the consecrations (saṃskāras) as previously described.
Regarding those who are incapable [of this], he says:
Alternatively, one should consecrate them with the four [rites] beginning with inspection;
inspection is performed with the root mantra, while sprinkling is considered to be done with the weapon mantra.
The sprinkling [of water] is performed with the *tāḍana-hetu* mantra and the weapon (*astra*) mantra.
In this sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), one should draw three lines extending toward the east and three lines extending toward the north.
The deity of the lines is stated in that very same place;
they are remembered as facing eastward, representing the gods, the directions, and Indra.
For the lines with their tips pointing northward, [the deities] are Brahmā, Vaivasvata (Yama), and the Moon;
or else, one should draw a hexagon, a triangle, a circle, and a square within the two sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*).
Therein, one should worship the Yoga-pīṭha according to the prescribed method.
p. 157a) Homage to Vāmā! Homage to Jyeṣṭhā! Homage to Raudrī! Homage to Ambikā!
One should worship these Śaktis above the girdle, starting from the east and so forth, having uttered: "Homage to Śrītārākuṇḍā!"
Thus she is to be worshipped.
In the center of that, one should worship the blue Sarasvatī, Tārā, Ṛtusnātā, and Vāgīśvarī.
Then, upon a seat made of gold or the like, or originating from jewels, or from the house of a learned Brahmin (śrotriya)—this is the rule.
"Vijenoddhṛtpānīya huṃ phaṭ! Svāhā to the flesh-eaters! Having thus completely offered [the portion] to the flesh-eaters, [one proceeds].

Having purified that [fire] with the *agnimantra*, veiled it with the *kavaca-mantra*, and displayed the *dhenumudrā*, one should turn it into nectar using the *varuṇabīja* and generate consciousness in the fire with the *param* mantra. Then, lifting it up with both hands and circling it three times, with knees resting on the surface of the earth, one should place it within the *kuṇḍa* with the thought that it is the seed-syllable of Śiva (*śivabīja*).
Having meditated upon the union of the Lord of Yogis (Śiva) and the Mistress of Speech (Śakti) within that womb,

one should cast the fire downward into that womb. Having worshipped with "Hrīṃ, obeisance to the form of Fire," one should utter the *hṛllekhā* mantra and draw [the breath] in through the *iḍā* [left nostril].

By means of the *kuṃbhaka* yoga, having joined the fire of the *bindu* located in the thousand-petaled lotus situated within the *suṣumnā* with the external stomach-fire by means of the *yonimudrā*, [one draws it] through the right channel (*dakṣiṇanāḍī*). (p. 158a)
Uttering *hṛllekhā*, one should expel the fire while uttering the *kūrcabīja* [HRĪM], saying: "Salutation to the consciousness of the fire (*vahnicaitanya*).

Thus, having joined that consciousness to the *garbhanāḍī* of Vāgīśvarī and having established it there, one should display the *jvālinī-mudrā*. Then, having covered the fire with sacrificial fuel and wood, one should kindle the fire with the *cinmantra*.
An example of a *cinmantra* is as follows:
*oṃ citpiṅgala hana 2 daha 2 paca 2 sarvajñā jñāpaya svāhā*. (p. 158b)
Oṃ. Then, having placed the fire upon the limb of Brahmā through the application of the root-mantra and so forth, one should worship it with devotion.
It is as follows:
"To the thousand-rayed one, homage to the heart; svasti to the full one, svāhā to the head; arise, O Puruṣa!"
*Śiṣāye vaṣaṭ*. *Dhūmavyāpine kavacāya huṃ*. *Saptajihvāya netratrayāya vauṣaṭ*.
*Dhanurdharāya astrāya phaṭ*. Having thus worshipped the limbs, [recite]: *Oṃ vaiśvānara jātaveda iha āvaha lohitākṣa sarvakarmāṇi sādhaya 2 svāhā*.
Having thus invoked with the root mantra, [one should visualize] piercing through the seat of the fire of Tārā with the *bhittva* [mantra]. (p.
Having given the name "Tārāgnirasitā," one should meditate upon the Fire-god (Agni).

Then, one should contemplate Agni as having seven hands, three feet, two heads, and four tusks; with his middle bound in three ways, endowed with tawny eyes numbering thirty-six, and shining with four ears.
He is seated upon a red lotus, with one foot dangling down;
he has mounted the back of a lordly bull facing him, and is endowed with four right arms, three of which are formidable.

One should meditate upon [the deity] holding a spear, a fire, a *śruk* and *śruva* ladles with his right hands, and a *tomara* lance and a palm-leaf fan with his left hands; [and] holding a vessel of molten gold filled with ghee, while constantly praising him, one should meditate on him as possessing seven tongues of flame.

Alternatively, one should meditate thus: [The deity] resembles the bandhūka flower, with the luster of well-refined gold; holding a lotus in his hand, adorned with two faces for the sake of instruction; possessing seven meters, a garment of sea-monsters (makara), and three bodies;
consisting of the three fires, having three feet, and the destroyer of both *havya* and *kavya* offerings.
The Brahma-ātman, the Sūryadagdha, the Tṛhotṛ, the fourfold Hī-virājita,

Having raised Kuṇḍalinī by means of the forward and reverse order accompanied by Meru, one should recite [the mantra].
As it is said in the Mātṛkā-rṇava:
"The rosary is declared to be fivefold; the thread consists of Śakti and the nature of Śiva."
The coiled power (Kuṇḍalinī-śakti) is knotted; at the end of the Kalās, she is established upon Meru.
Now, the fire sacrifice (homa):
In the navel-pit, where Kuṇḍalinī is the fire and latent impressions are the fuel, while the supreme nectar is the oblation, one should offer with the ladle of bliss.
One should offer the functions of the senses with the mantra that is about to be recited.
The mantra is as follows:

Having recited the root mantra, [one should offer] a single oblation with "Svāhā," mentally offering the activity of the blue syllable into the fire whose nature is consciousness at the navel-mandala, which is the lamp of knowledge, using the mind as the sacrificial ladle. Then, having recited the root mantra again...
With the mind as the sacrificial ladle, he offers the oblations of merit and demerit into the fire whose form is radiant.
"By means of the path of the Suṣumṇā, I perpetually offer the functioning of the senses;
Svāhā!"—this is the second oblation.
The Root Mantra:
With the hands of light and space, using myself as the sacrificial ladle, I offer into the full fire the clarified butter of merit and demerit along with their fruits— svāhā!

I offer the universe— beginning with the earth and ending with the quarters of space— into the fire of consciousness, which blazes forth as an uninterrupted internal bond, which acts as an adversary to the darkness of illusion, and which serves as the ground for the rays that illuminate the Self.
Now, regarding Yoga:

it has been stated in the *Haṃsapārameśvara-tantra*: "O fair-faced one, listen to the supreme Yoga which is declared as the Supreme Brahman. In the foundation (ādhāra), at the location of the anus, there is a four-petalled lotus."
The Yoni, known as Kāmākhyā, the supreme Mistress, resides within the pericarp; indeed, the manifest Kaṃdarpa is in the Ādhāra, which is triangular.
O Dear One, within the self-manifested liṅga, it faces west;
two finger-breadths above that and two finger-breadths below is the center.
In its center, one finger-breadth wide, is a square with a triangle;
in the middle of that is the station of Śikhin, resembling molten gold.
Resembling the bandhūka flower and flashing like a streak of lightning,
it is endowed with seven-rayed flames and contains within its womb the fire of time and Rudra.
From the letter 'A' to the letter 'Kṣa', endowed with the ten kalās—this is declared to be Agni; now I shall describe Sūrya to you.
In the region of the bladder, O highly fortunate one, situated at the base of the middle [channel],
is the seed-syllable resembling vermilion, like a ripe pomegranate.
There, O Goddess of the Gods, the Sun should know [the mantra] joined with twelve digits;
the twelve seed-syllables beginning with the digit [Ka], arranged in pairs of two.
In the midst of that, O highly fortunate one, is the Rajas-śakti, resembling the rising sun; the world is situated within the solar wind.
The head-bindu is renowned as the mind-moon;
the first seed-syllable is the unmanī, and the sky is fourfold.
The primordial seed is the great space; the mind becomes one's own moon.
Unmanī is the breath-moon, the destroyer of the Mitra-moon.
Then the yogi, consisting of all moonlight, should practice meditation;
[he should contemplate] that subtle crest-lock (śikhā) situated in the syllable Oṃ, which is the digit (kalā) whose nature is consciousness and which is one with the Self.
Contemplating that supreme state, one should firmly press the tongue against the palate and meditate upon the self as having become one with the subtle [principle].
O Dear One, through union with the mouth of Hara, that crest-lock (śikhā) shall increase;
then, having pierced the Brahma-knot, the head of the Kula-lineage is severed.
The vital air enters the *suṣumnā* at the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*) and proceeds through the middle channel;
then, having pierced the *svādhiṣṭhāna*, it enters both ears.
O Beloved, in the region of the navel is the abode of Brahmā, known as Maṇipūra;
from there, one whose movement is constant should pierce that pure sphere consisting of blazing light.
Above that is the station of Viṣṇu, radiant as the petal of a blue lotus;
having pierced the heart-center known as the Brahma-granthi, which consists of two or three strands.
Then, having performed the skillful rite, she [pierced] the root of the palate which is of the nature of the vowels;
then, having broken through the abode of Rudra, Maheśvarī reached the forehead.
Māheśvarī, having reached the digit of the moon on Mount Meru, which is the cause of obstruction,
and having attained the mind of Śaṅkhinī, she sustains the bone that is empty of [dualistic] existence.
If one does not die while situated in the creation characterized by supreme bliss,
[one beholds] the great thousand-petaled lotus, adorned with red filaments.
O beloved, it has the luster of molten red lotus, with a downpour of falling streams;
situated in the midst of the great ocean, it is dark blue and filled with milk.
Listen to what is proclaimed regarding the upper foundation (ūrdhvādhāra): it is that very Nirañjana, who is identical with [the Self].
There, with a concentrated mind, one should meditate upon the Goddess who consists of eternal bliss;
O Dear One, one should cause the nectar to flow from the thousand-petaled lotus.
Having drunk, having drunk again, and having drunk once more, one should cause it to enter the *mūlādhāra*.
Having again drunk the nectar of the *kula*, one should once more enter the *kula*.
O Dear One, one should enter the unagitated thousand-spoked wheel at the station of the Goddess;
then, having again pierced the twelve syllables by means of the binding of the Yoni-mudrā.
Having drunk [the nectar] again through the Piṅgalā at the Mūlādhāra, O Sovereign of the Gods, one reaches the Garden situated between the two qualities and the Vastinādikā.
Likewise, Jālandhara is in the mouth, Kāmarūpaka in the palate,
Pūrṇagiri in the center of the heart, and Śrīhṛd above the uvula.

One should worship the wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpataru*)— which grants the desired accomplishments of the practitioner— located upon the neck, the full mountain-base, and situated on the head, within the garden of the eon (*kalpodyāna*).
O Dear One, the wise declare that at the root of the tree of the letters (lipitaru) is the Goddess, and that the tree itself is composed of eternal phonemes within its lotus-like heart.
The great seed-syllable consisting of the letter *sa*, the Great Śiva of Bindu and Nāda,
has fully blossomed in all directions with branches that are the imperishable syllables of the earth.
The three worlds were covered with vessels containing nectar and medicinal herbs,
blazing with clusters of fire-colored gems like the celestial wish-fulfilling tree.
He illuminated that city with the splendor of the Maruts through excellent *tulasī* flowers;
he whose eyes were like the fruits of the celestial ocean was the supreme glory of all beings.
I bow to that Supreme Goddess, who is described by the Vedas, Agamas, and other scriptures as being most exalted and captivating to the mind, [and who is like] great nectar, eyes, and honey.

The Goddess meditated upon the three worlds as being directly composed of Śiva and Śakti, resting within her shadow, and rooted in that [divine couple] who are the mothers of all the lords of the quarters.
Why would these not be accomplished on this earth by mere thought?
Also, in the *Tantrarāja*,
in the section on the general yoga:
Visualizing the supreme nectar-producing Vidyā situated in the center of the head,
one should recite it with a one-pointed mind.

From the mandala, the perfection of poetry shall arise, as well as mastery over all languages; and in all matters such as debate and the like, one who has become the very self of the deity shall be victorious.
In the *Sakalajananī-stotra*:
"O Goddess whose nature is bliss, there is no place where Your form—which consists of sound (*nāda*)—is not pervaded;
I praise that form which is perceived by the internal mind and which the blessed proclaim through tears and horripilation."
One should not mock him as prescribed in the scriptures;
rather, those who know his vital points should offer him the "hero's joined palms" (añjali) as a sign of submission.
This *Vāsanādinirṇaya* was written by Śaṅkara, the grandson of Lambodara and the son of Kamalākara.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Underlying Intentions," in the *Tantracūḍāmaṇi*, which is the *Tārārahasyavṛtti* composed by the venerable Śaṅkarācārya. 15.
Auspicious!
